La Commission elle-même a sans aucun doute adoptée la position la plus stricte quant à la prohibition pour les juridictions militaires d'exercer compétence sur les civils. Cette posture s'est manifestée tant par des édits jurisprudentiels qu'à l'occasion de l'examen des rapports des Etats.

Pour ce qui est de la jurisprudence, la Commission a adopté une approche péremptoire et constante. Ainsi, dans sa décision de principe Law Office of Ghazi Suleiman c. Sudan, la Commission n'admet aucune exception à la compétence personnelle des tribunaux militaires « dont la mission est de connaître des infractions de nature purement militaire commises par un personnel strictement militaire ». Une telle position jurisprudentielle se fondait, entre autres, sur ce que la composition, les relations hiérarchiques et les procédures adoptées devant les juridictions militaires ne peuvent fournir les garanties minimales nécessaires à un procès équitable, à l'égalité devant la loi et à l'indépendance de la justice. De manière non-équivoque, la Commission estime, comme elle l'a décidé par exemple dans l'affaire Media Rights Agenda c. Nigeria, que le fait pour des tribunaux militaires de juger des civils viole les dispositions de l'article 7 de la Charte africaine.

En phase avec cette position jurisprudentielle, la Commission n'a eu de cesse, à l'occasion de l'examen des rapports des Etats, d'insister sur la prohibition impérative de la compétence des tribunaux militaires sur les civils. Par exemple, dans ses Observations finales suite à l'examen des Rapports périodiques de l'Ouganda en 2006 et 2009, la Commission en appelait urgemment à l'Etat sous examen de proscrire expressément dans sa législation, le jugement de personnes civiles par des juridictions militaires. L'appel de la Commission faisait suite au refus du Gouvernement d'Ouganda d'exécuter les décisions de la Cour constitutionnelle et de la Cour suprême qui avaient déclaré en violation de la Constitution, le jugement par la Cour martiale de civils agriculteurs-éleveurs Karamojong pour activité terroriste et usage d'armes.

En l'espèce, la Commission constate que l'Etat défendeur a légalement prévu et autorisé le jugement des victimes par le Tribunal militaire de Yaoundé. A la lumière de la jurisprudence ainsi rappelée, une telle autorisation viole manifestement le droit international pertinent auquel est partie la République du Cameroun, en particulier les dispositions de l'article 7(1)(a) de la Charte africaine.

En ce qui concerne l'allégation de violation du droit à la défense protégé par l'article 7(1)(c) de la Charte africaine, la Commission rappelle qu'il est d'une obligation fondamentale pour les juridictions de communiquer avec l'accusé dans une langue qu'il comprend, tout le long de la procédure. Le moyen tiré de l'obligation constitutionnelle pour tout citoyen camerounais de comprendre l'Anglais et le Français ne saurait par conséquent prospérer. En se référant à ses Directives et principes sur le droit à un procès équitable, la Commission note que le devoir incombant à l'Etat en la matière est de fournir à la personne accusée des services de traduction et d'interprétariat dans la langue qu'elle comprend. En l'espèce, les victimes étaient toutes anglophones et se sont plaintes d'avoir été interrogées en français.

A cet égard, l'Etat défendeur se rapporte au 24 rôle du jugement no 230/99 du 5 octobre 1999 pour prouver que les victimes ont bien eu droit à l'assistance de deux interprètes. Cette allégation n'est pas réfutée par le Plaignant qui soulève plutôt l'application de deux procédures, l'une accusatoire et l'autre inquisitoire, sans pour autant réussir à contrer l'assignation d'interprètes prouvée par l'Etat défendeur. Le moyen invoqué par le Plaignant sur ce point spécifique n'ayant pu être suffisamment soutenu, la Commission ne peut conclure à une violation de l'article 7(1)(c) de la Charte africaine.

Enfin, le Plaignant allègue la violation du droit protégé par l'article 7(1)(d), d'être jugé dans un délai raisonnable par un tribunal impartial. Sur les moyens tirés de cette violation, la Commission rappelle que, sans donner une définition spécifique de la notion de délai raisonnable, elle a constamment évalué le délai raisonnable des procédures internes selon les circonstances de chaque cause, donc au cas par cas. Ainsi, la Commission a retenu comme anormalement longues des procédures ayant duré dix, cinq et deux ans, sur la base notamment des prescriptions du droit interne de l'Etat défendeur, du comportement des autorités et du Plaignant, des faits de la cause et de la situation particulière des Plaignants.

Sur la question de l'imputabilité à l'Etat défendeur de la durée anormalement longue des procédures internes, la Commission a constamment conclu que des circonstances particulières surmontables ne peuvent être invoquées pour justifier un retard manifestement préjudiciable aux droits du justiciable. Par exemple, la Commission décidait dans l'affaire Pagnoule (pour le compte de Mazou) c. Cameroun, qu'un procès ayant duré deux ans sans que le moindre acte de procédure ait été accompli par la Cour suprême viole le droit d'être jugé dans un délai raisonnable. La Commission procède à un examen plus approfondi de la question dans la décision Article 19 c. Eritrée où elle considère que ni la gravité ou la complexité des crimes allégués, ni l'encombrement du rôle de la juridiction de jugement, ni la situation politique à l'intérieur de l'Etat défendeur ne peuvent justifier une derogation au droit d'être jugé dans un délai raisonnable.

En l'espèce, la Commission note que l'Etat défendeur ne conteste pas que la Cour d'appel a accusé un retard en n'examinant la requête des victimes que près de sept ans après son introduction. Cependant, la défense de l'Etat est fondée principalement sur le défaut pour le Président de la République de nommer une partie des juges devant siéger dans la composition de la juridiction d'appel.

A cet égard, la Commission fait observer que selon le principe général d'équité et de justice, le retard encouru dans les procédures devant les juridictions internes sont de plein droit imputables à l'Etat. Un tel retard ne saurait par conséquent causer préjudice aux justiciables. De l'avis de la Commission, il n'y a aucun doute que le fait pour l'Etat défendeur d'avoir mis plus de cinq années à procéder à des nominations a eu un impact direct sur le délai dans lequel les victimes devaient être fixées sur leur sort. En effet, les appelants auraient pu, par exemple, avoir été remis en liberté si la Cour d'appel avait examiné leur pourvoi dans un délai raisonnable.

Sur ce même point, la Commission note que la situation ne s'est pas améliorée dans la suite de la procédure au plan interne, concernant notamment le pourvoi toujours pendant devant la Cour suprême. En effet, plus de cinq années se sont écoulées après le pourvoi en cassation sans que le moindre acte ou la moindre décision n'ait été pris. En conséquence, les violations subies dès la décision du Tribunal militaire ont été aggravées par l'Etat défendeur puisque les victimes se sont vues dénier le droit de contester une décision manifestement contraire aux obligations internationales de la République du Cameroun. Les victimes ont ainsi été forcées de purger des peines alors même que les procédures étaient prolongées indéfiniment. La Commission estime qu'une telle situation équivalerait à paralyser les recours légaux existant dans le but potentiel de faire purger des peines prononcées en violation du droit international des droits de l'homme. Dans ces circonstances, la justice n'a pu être rendue dans un délai raisonnable comme le prescrivent les dispositions pertinentes de l'article 7(1)(d).

Sur la violation alléguée du droit d'être jugé par un tribunal impartial, la Commission note qu'elle a déjà constaté le caractère peremptoire de la prohibition faite aux juridictions militaires de juger des personnes civiles. Dans la jurisprudence de référence, la Commission a constamment conclu qu'une telle interdiction est fondée principalement sur le défaut d'impartialité et d'indépendance inhérent aux tribunaux militaires lorsqu'ils ont compétence pour juger les civils. Au demeurant, et sans qu'il soit plus besoin de s'attarder sur les moyens subsequent, la Commission constate que les dispositions de l'article 7(1)(d) de la Charte africaine n'ont pas été respectées.

En sus d'une décision concluant à la violation des dispositions des articles 5 et 7 de la Charte africaine, le Plaignant demande à la Commission d'ordonner à la République du Cameroun de payer la somme totale de 3 000 000 000 (trois milliards) FCFA à l'ensemble des dix-huit victimes.

Ayant conclu à la violation des dispositions des articles 5, 7(1)(a) et 7(1)(d) de la Charte africaine, la Commission doit se prononcer sur la demande de réparation faite par le Plaignant. La Commission reconnaît le principe inhérent du droit à réparation pour les préjudices soufferts par suite d'une violation des dispositions de la Charte africaine. La Commission est d'avis qu'une suite doit être faite à la demande en compensation monétaire lorsque le Plaignant ou les victimes en font une tel que c'est le cas en l'espèce. La Commission rappelle en outre, qu'à la lumière de sa jurisprudence, l'évaluation du quantum d'une telle compensation est laissée aux juridictions ou autorités nationales de l'Etat défendeur.

Cependant, la Commission fait observer que la discrétion des autorités compétentes de l'Etat défendeur quant à l'évaluation du quantum des réparations doit s'exercer dans le respect des normes minimales acceptées au plan international. Ainsi, toute évaluation doit être guidée par le principe du restitutio in integrum, soit à replacer la victime dans la position antérieure à la violation autant que possible. Dans les cas où la restitution est impossible, l'Etat défendeur peut recourir séparément ou cumulativement à la compensation, à la réhabilitation et à d'autres modes de réparation. En cas de disparition ou de décès, la réparation doit aller au bénéfice des ayants-droits de la victime. Enfin, toute réparation doit être juste, adéquate, efficace, suffisante, appropriée, orientée vers la victime et proportionnelle au préjudice souffert.

La Commission note que les Parties s'accordent sur ce que les peines initiales prononcées à l'encontre des victimes par le Tribunal militaire de Yaoundé en 1999 varient de huit (08) à vingt (20) ans d'emprisonnement et la prison à vie. Des informations soumises par les Parties, il ressort que la durée totale de détention a excédé le quantum des peines prononcées par la première juridiction pour plusieurs d'entre les victimes. Les victimes condamnées à des peines inférieures à la durée totale de détention ont par conséquent dû être remises en liberté après avoir purgé la peine, puisque les procédures se sont prolongées. En revanche, les victimes condamnées à des peines supérieures devraient toujours être dans les liens de la détention.

Sur la base des constatations précédentes, la Commission considère qu'en ce qui concerne les actes de torture et de traitements inhumains, une réparation pécuniaire est à la fois appropriée et indispensable pour panser les plaies des victimes. S'agissant de la violation des dispositions des 7(1)(a) et 7(1)(d), la Commission note qu'à la date de la Plainte en 2004, les victimes avaient déjà été détenues pendant sept années alors que leur pourvoi en appel était maintenu en souffrance du fait de l'inaction des autorités de l'Etat défendeur.

Ceci dit, la détention s'étant poursuivie pendant la procédure devant la Cour suprême, il doit s'ensuivre une computation conséquente, en particulier pour les personnes toujours détenues à la date de la présente décision. En effet, à la date de sa décision, la Commission n'avait reçu de l'Etat défendeur aucune indication de ce que la Cour suprême avait délibéré. Dans tous les cas, la compétence attribuée au Tribunal militaire de Yaoundé pour juger les victimes n'étant pas conforme aux obligations internationales de l'Etat défendeur, les peines prononcées par ladite juridiction sont frappées par le même défaut de conformité.

En conséquence des violations constatées et en application des principes d'équité et de justice, il s'impose une compensation adéquate et suffisante pour les personnes ayant purgé tout ou partie de la peine initiale. S'agissant des personnes toujours en détention, eu égard au caractère non-conforme à la Charte africaine du jugement du Tribunal militaire et au temps de souffrance et de privation de liberté déjà enduré dans les conditions constatées par la Commission, il s'impose en sus une remise en liberté, pure et simple.

La Commission note qu'aux termes des dispositions de l'article 112(2) de son Règlement intérieur, lorsque la décision a été rendue contre un Etat défendeur, les parties doivent, dans un délai de cent quatre vingt (180) jours à compter de la notification de la décision, informer par écrit la Commission de toutes mesures prises ou qui sont en train d'être prises par l'Etat défendeur pour donner effet à la décision. La Commission, Par ces motifs,
Dit que la République du Cameroun n'a pas violé les dispositions de l'article 7(1)(c) de la Charte africaine.

Déclare, en revanche, que la République du Cameroun a violé les dispositions des articles 5, 7(1)(a) et 7(1)(d) de la Charte africaine. En conséquence : i. Demande instamment à la République du Cameroun de prendre les mesures nécessaires à la libération immédiate, pure et simple, de toutes les personnes toujours en détention. ii. Demande par ailleurs à la République du Cameroun de verser à toutes les victimes ou à leurs ayants-droits une indemnisation appropriée, juste et adéquate. Le montant de l'indemnisation sera calculé en prenant en compte le pretium doloris du fait des actes de torture et traitements inhumains, le préjudice souffert du fait de la détention, la durée de la procédure et les impenses. iii. Recommande vivement à la République du Cameroun de prendre les mesures nécessaires à l'effet de punir les responsables des actes de torture et de traitements inhumains subis par les victimes. iv. Recommande en outre à la République du Cameroun d'assurer au sein de ses institutions compétentes, particulièrement les institutions d'exécution de la loi et les établissements de détention, une meilleure connaissance et une application stricte du droit international pertinent et de la législation nationale sur la torture et les traitements cruels, inhumains et dégradants. v. Recommande urgemment à la République du Cameroun de mettre sa législation sur l'organisation judiciaire en conformité avec la Charte africaine et ses obligations internationales en matière de droits de l'homme en rétrocédant pleine et exclusive compétence aux juridictions de droit commun pour juger les personnes civiles. vi. Demande enfin à la République du Cameroun de lui rapporter par écrit, dans les cent quatre vingt jours (180) jours de la notification de la présente décision, quant aux mesures entreprises à l'effet de la mise en œuvre de ces recommandations. Adoptée lors de la 15 Session extra-ordinaire de la Commission Africaine des Droits de l'Homme et des Peuples, tenue du 7 au 14 mars 2014, à Banjul, Gambie.

On 12 May 2004, the Secretariat of the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights (the Secretariat) received from Counsel Titanji Duga Ernest, lawyer at the firm Duga and Co. based in Yaoundé, Cameroon, a Complaint submitted on the basis of Article 55 of the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights (the African Charter).

The Complaint was submitted against the Republic of Cameroon (State Party to the African Charter and hereinafter referred to as the Respondent State or the Republic of Cameroon), in the name and on behalf of eighteen (18) persons in detention named as follows: Cheonumu Martin, Neba Wilson, Neba Samuel, Njakoy Charles Chin, Ngek Adelberth W., Nyamsai Promise, Ngoh Jop Bulewah, Ntanen Daniel Ndifon, Fonkwah Thomas Chin, Tete Philip, Atambun Geh Sama, Khan Zachariah Ndifet, Julius Ngu Ndi, Akwanga Ebenezer, Tata Roland Ndze, Ngek Simon Kwei, Lukong Hassan and Jumven Edwin. These persons are all members of the Southern Camerouns' National Council (SCNC).

The Complainant states that in March 1997, the above-mentioned persons were arrested on different dates, in the North-West province of the Republic of Cameroon where they were suspected of conducting secessionist activities and detained in different gendarmerie cells. The Complainant continues that the victims were allegedly tortured for the purpose of extorting confessions, before being transferred to another jurisdiction in Yaoundé (about 400 kilometres from the initial place of detention). None of the victims would remember the date of the said transfer owing to the inhuman conditions of their detention. They were allegedly then incarcerated in the Kondengui high security prison.

After about 24 months of mental and physical torture, they were charged and transferred to the Military Tribunal of Yaoundé where they were indicted on 15 February 1999. Their trial lasted about 9 months and, on 5 October 1999, they were sentenced to terms of imprisonment ranging from 8 years' imprisonment to life imprisonment. The persons thus convicted all immediately appealed the decision but, since 1999, no action has been taken on their appeals. According to the Complainant, all contacts, exceptional negotiations and formal requests have remained without effect and even the interventions of the National Commission on Human Rights and Freedoms of Cameroon since 2003 have produced no result.

The Complainant finally reports that one of the detainees, Ntanen Daniel Ndifon, died in detention while another, Akwanga Ebenezor, who was seriously ill, is reported missing. This has caused the Complainant to fear that the detainees may be systematically eliminated one after another.

The Complainant alleges the violation of Articles 5 and 7 of the African Charter. He requests the Commission to order the Republic of Cameroon to pay the total sum of 3,000,000,000 CFA francs to all the victims for the violations thus alleged.

The Complaint reached the Secretariat on 12 May 2004. At its 35th Ordinary Session held from 21 May to 4 June 2004 in Banjul, The Gambia, the Commission considered it and decided to be seized of it. The Commission also decided to send an Urgent Appeal to the President of the Republic. On 17 June 2004, the Secretariat informed the Parties of this decision and requested them to transmit their observations on admissibility before the 36th Ordinary Session.

On 21 and 23 September 2004, the Secretariat received the observations of the Complainant and of the State on admissibility respectively. The Secretariat exchanged the pleadings between the Parties, on 11 and 13 October 2004 respectively.

At its 36th Ordinary Session, the Commission considered the Communication and declared it admissible. In February 2005, the Secretariat informed the Parties of this decision and requested their submissions. Copies of the Complaint and of subsequent correspondence were also handed to the delegation of the Respondent State during a visit to the Secretariat on 31 March 2005.
On 12 April 2005, the Chairperson of the Commission, through the High Commission of Cameroon in Dakar, Senegal, requested the President of the Republic of Cameroon to take provisional measures.

At the 37th Ordinary Session held from 27 April to 11 May 2005 in Banjul, The Gambia, the Commission considered the present Communication and decided to defer its decision on the merits to the 38th Ordinary Session to allow the Respondent State to prepare its observations on the merits. On 7 May 2005, the Secretariat duly informed the Parties thereof. On 12 September 2005, the Secretariat sent a reminder correspondence to the Respondent State.

At its 38th Ordinary Session held from 21 November to 5 December 2005 in Banjul, The Gambia, the Commission considered the Communication and deferred its decision to the 39th Ordinary Session. By correspondences dated 30 January and 5 February 2006, the Secretariat informed the Parties of this decision.

At its 39th Ordinary Session held from 11 to 25 May 2006 in Banjul, The Gambia, the Commission considered the Communication and decided to defer it to the 40th Ordinary Session to allow the State to submit its observations on the merits. The Parties were duly informed thereof.

Following a public hearing held on 25 November 2006 during its 40th Ordinary Session, the Commission deferred consideration of the Communication on the merits given that the Respondent State argued that it had not received notification of the decision on admissibility. On 6 December 2006 and 16 April 2007, the Secretariat sent reminder correspondences to the Respondent State while transmitting to it a copy of the decision on admissibility. On 30 April 2007, the Respondent State transmitted its observations on the merits, a copy of which was given to the Complainant on 2 May 2007. The Complainant transmitted his reply on 6 May 2007.
At its 43rd Ordinary Session held from 7 to 22 May 2008, the Commission considered the Communication and deferred its decision on the merits to the 44th Ordinary Session for lack of time.

On 7 May 2010, the Complainant informed the Secretariat of new deaths among the victims on whose behalf the Communication had been submitted. In this regard, the Complainant mentioned the names of Martin Cheonomu, Julius Ngu Ndi, Philip Tete and Zachariah Khan.

The Communication was the subject of successive deferrals, of an examination at the 51st Ordinary Session of the Commission held from 9 to 22 October 2012 and then of a further deferral. The Parties were informed thereof. THE LAW Admissibility The Complainant's arguments on Admissibility

While alleging that the Communication complies with all the requirements of Article 56 of the African Charter, the Complainant particularly insists on compliance with the rule of exhaustion of local remedies. In support of this argument, the Complainant reports that the appeal on behalf of the victims was lodged in 1999 and that, more than five years later, there was still no follow-up to the said request and no written judgment had been rendered. He concludes that the Commission should, in the present case, apply an exception to compliance with Article 56(5) and declare the Communication admissible.

By its arguments on Admissibility, the Respondent State calls on the African Commission to declare the Communication inadmissible for insufficient identification of the authors of the Communication, non-exhaustion of local remedies and consideration of the matter by another international body. With regard to the first point, the Respondent State argues that since the Communication does not sufficiently identify its authors, in particular with regard to their age and profession, it is not compatible with Rule 104(1)(a) of the Commission's Rules of Procedure.

On the second point, the Respondent State argues that the delay in the appeal proceedings was due neither to the alleged unavailability of the copy of the decision of the first court nor to an intention to deny the applicants the right to appeal that judgment. According to the State, the time that elapsed was necessary to satisfy the condition of the appointment by the President of the Republic of the additional judges to sit in the appellate court. While acknowledging the said delay, the State rather disputes its unduly long nature.

Finally, on the third argument, the Respondent State argues that the victims did indeed submit the matter to the United Nations Commission on Human Rights, which had decided that the allegations of torture were unfounded. The State concludes that the Commission cannot consider the present Communication without violating the provisions of Article 56(7) of the African Charter.

The present Communication was submitted in accordance with Article 55 of the African Charter which gives competence to the Commission to receive and consider communications other than those of States Parties. Such communications must, in order to be declared admissible, fulfil the conditions provided for in Article 56 of the African Charter.

From the examination of the arguments invoked by the Parties, the Commission notes that the three issues raised by the State are in dispute. The Commission finds by itself that the Communication complies with the other conditions laid down in Article 56 of the African Charter. The analysis on Admissibility therefore concerns the three issues mentioned above.

Under the provisions of Article 56(1) of the African Charter, Communications submitted to the Commission must indicate their author, even if the latter requests anonymity. The reason for this requirement is to enable the Commission: to remain in communication with the author, to know his identity and situation, to be assured of the continuation of his interest in the Communication and to request additional information, where appropriate, as reflected in Rule 104 of the Commission's Rules of Procedure.

The Commission observes that Rule 104(1)(a) does not contain a mandatory requirement. Its provisions should be invoked by the Commission when one of the Parties requests anonymity. The Commission notes, however, that the information identifying the author of the Communication is essentially intended for it since it cannot be disclosed to the Respondent State when anonymity is requested.

In the view of the Commission, the Communication contains sufficient information to identify the author and the victims on whose behalf it is submitted. Consequently, the Commission cannot uphold the Respondent State on this argument. The Commission concludes that the Communication complies with the provisions of Article 56(1) of the African Charter.

As regards the provisions of Article 56(5) of the African Charter, they require that Communications be admissible only when the Complainant has exhausted the available local remedies unless these remedies have been unduly prolonged. The rationale for this condition is that before seizing an international forum, the Respondent State should have the opportunity to redress the damage caused to the victim by its own means and within the framework of its judicial system. However, the Commission has also considered that compliance with this principle does not imply that the Complainant must necessarily exhaust remedies where these are not available.

In the present case, the Commission notes that, as confirmed by the Respondent State, the delay in the domestic proceedings is not contested. The appeal lodged by the Complainant has been pending before the Cameroonian courts for five (05) years, proof that the Respondent State has been amply informed of the situation of the victims. The Commission is of the view that this is unequivocally an undue prolongation implying that, although the remedy was available in theory, it was not effective. In these circumstances, the Commission cannot uphold the Respondent State's objection based on non-exhaustion of local remedies.

Finally, an examination of the provisions of Article 56(7) shows that the said provisions refer to “cases which have been settled” and not to matters brought before another international body. In its arguments on this point, the Respondent State does not indicate whether the matter was settled on the merits or not by the United Nations Human Rights Committee. The related argument is limited to reporting that the State argued before the UN Body that the victims had not suffered acts of torture and/or inhuman treatment during their detention.

Moreover, the Respondent State provided no details concerning the time at which the matter was submitted to the Human Rights Committee nor any document relating to a decision, if any. The Commission considers that the mere allegations of the Respondent State are not sufficient to conclude that the provisions of Article 52(7) of the African Charter have not been complied with. Such allegations of fact must be supported by specific information to enable the Commission to conclude.

Finally, the material scope of the Communication submitted to the Commission extends well beyond the allegation of torture and/or inhuman treatment. The Communication moreover alleges violations of the rights linked to a fair trial regarding which the Respondent State likewise gives no indication as to their settlement by the UN Body. Consequently, the Commission considers that the present case has not been settled within the terms of Article 56(7).

In the light of the foregoing, the Commission concludes that Communication 287/04 initiated by Ernest Duga Titanji (on behalf of Cheonumu Martin and Others) against the Republic of Cameroon fulfils the conditions of Article 56 of the African Charter and consequently declares it admissible.

Article 5 of the African Charter protects, among other things, the right to the dignity of the person and prohibits physical or moral torture, and cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment or treatment. According to the Complainant, the fact that the victims were beaten and refused any medical treatment - which had resulted in the death of at least one of them at the date of the seizure of the Commission - constitutes a violation of Article 5 of the Charter.

On the point of evidence, the Complainant alleges that the medical certificate attesting to the effects of torture on the deceased victims could not be produced since any medical intervention was refused. In order to establish proof, the Complainant requests the Commission to invoke the provisions of Article 46 of the Charter which provide that it may, in proceedings pending before it, resort to any appropriate method of investigation. In the Complainant's understanding, his inability to produce any evidence is the consequence of the fact that the victims were still, at the date of the submission of the present Communication, in detention in a maximum security prison.

In support of the argument based on the violation of Article 7 of the African Charter, the Complainant alleges that the “right to appeal to competent national organs” was not protected. The Complainant thus argues that the persons concerned by the present Communication were first denied the right to appeal and that their appeal lodged in 1999 was examined only seven years later without any follow-up being given to it nonetheless. He further reports that the correspondences addressed by their Counsel and by the National Commission on Human Rights and Freedoms of Cameroon with a view to having their file transmitted to the Court of Appeal remained unanswered.

Regarding the outcome of the proceedings initiated at the domestic level, the Complainant argues that between 1999 and the seizure of the Commission in 2004, no written judgment was rendered by the Cameroonian courts to enable the victims to exercise their right to appeal. Citing the jurisprudence of the United Nations Human Rights Committee, among others, in the case of Champagne and Others v. Jamaica (Communication No. 445/1991, 18 July 1994), the Complainant argues that, even if a written judgment were to be rendered after several years, it might not reflect the trial proceedings.

The Complainant also pleads the right to the presumption of innocence and the lack of jurisdiction of the court that dealt with the victims' case. On this point, he observes that the persons concerned are members of the SCNC, a movement composed of English-speaking Cameroonians advocating the secession of what they call “the Republic of Cameroon”, which would have violated the terms of the unitary Constitution. The Complainant argues that the fact that the victims were removed from Bamenda, the jurisdiction that should have had competence over their case, to be tried in a court located in the francophone part constitutes proof of the partiality of this forum. The reason, according to the Complainant, is that the victims speak only English but were tried by a court whose language of proceedings is French and, consequently, the trial could not have been impartial.
Finally, the Complainant alleges that the victims did not benefit from justice within a reasonable time, the related procedure having lasted seven years without any outcome.

Without significantly contesting the facts as reported by the Complainant, the Respondent State raises, at the outset of the proceedings on the merits, an objection of non-communication of the decision on admissibility. In support of this objection, the State argues that the Commission's decisions on admissibility are liable to be based on elements of both fact and law that may influence the defence on the merits.

In the alternative, the State nevertheless submits on the merits of the Communication. In response to the allegations of violation of Article 5 of the African Charter, the State refers to the provisions of both the Constitution and the Penal Code to argue that the Cameroonian legislative and judicial framework was sufficiently dissuasive at the time of the events. According to the State, the officers of the investigation and detention services were amply warned to avoid the acts alleged by the Complainant. That the Complainant lodged no complaint for torture constitutes, the State alleges, proof of the compliance by the said officers with the prohibitions laid down by domestic law.

Moreover, the State considers that the Complainant produced no evidence of the nature and substance of the alleged acts of torture and that the national authorities had discretion in the conduct of the investigation provided that it was not arbitrary. With regard to the lack of medical care, the State reports that the applicants' place of detention had an infirmary and the possibility of evacuation to other establishments in the town.

The State alleges the competence of the Military Tribunal of Yaoundé by recalling that under an amendment in 1997 of the 1972 law on judicial organisation, civil courts are divested, in favour of military courts, of cases relating to offences under the legislation on weapons of war. The State considers that, the victims being accused of such offences which resulted in the death of public officials, the other offences were connected in accordance with the Criminal Investigation Code and that the competence of the Military Tribunal was amply justified.

With regard to the lack of local jurisdiction alleged by the Complainant, the Respondent State argues that by virtue of the subsequent creation of a national-jurisdiction Military Tribunal sitting in Yaoundé, the said court can hear any case, regardless of the place where the facts were committed. The Respondent State thus argues that the trial had been relocated for legal reasons of serenity and efficiency of the procedure. As regards the independence of military justice, the State justifies it by regulatory provisions, by the training of military magistrates at the National School of Magistracy and by judicial precedents proving the knowledge of human rights by the Cameroonian military judge.

In response to the fact that the victims were not tried in a language they understand, the State recalls the constitutional duty incumbent on every Cameroonian to understand both English and French. The State further alleges that the victims did have the right to the assistance of two interpreters both at the stage of prosecution and at that of the trial before the Military Tribunal.

Finally, the Respondent State, while acknowledging the delay recorded in the examination of the case, alleges that such a delay cannot be characterised as excessive. In this regard, the State reports that in compliance with the legislation applicable at the time of the events, it was imperative to include in the composition of the Court of Appeal an assessor whereas all the available assessors had reached the age limit and been retired. The process of replacing them required, according to the State's allegations, a reasonable time.

As a preliminary to the analysis on the merits, the Commission addresses the main objection raised by the Respondent State, that the decision on admissibility was not communicated to it. Referring to the procedure, the Commission notes that in February 2005, the Secretariat had handed to the delegation of the Respondent State copies of both the decision on admissibility and the correspondences relating to the Communication. Moreover, by at least two Notes Verbales dated 6 December 2006 and 16 April 2007, the State was notified again of the said decision. That said, the Commission notes that, by the said decision, it was satisfied that the Complaint complied with the requirements contested by the Respondent State, namely, the identification of the authors, the exhaustion of local remedies and the absence of lis pendens.

In any event, the Commission notes that by the objection it raises, the Respondent State mainly suggests the possibility for the decision on admissibility to steer the defence on the merits. In this regard, the Commission finds that this fear is unfounded since the State has indeed, in its arguments on the merits, replied to all the questions in dispute, in an equitable and satisfactory manner. Moreover, and since the State did submit on the substance of the alleged violations, the Commission is of the view that the case is ready and that it can examine its merits.

Article 5 of the African Charter protects, among other things, the right not to be subjected to physical or moral torture and to cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment or treatment. Without significantly calling into question the facts as reported by the Complainant, the Respondent State rather contests the nature of the acts complained of and guarantees the existence in its legislation of provisions that punish acts of torture.

As regards the nature of the acts liable to constitute torture, the Commission refers to the jurisprudence of the High Court of Zambia in the Banda case to note that punishments such as “lashes with a whip or sticks” were considered rather as inhuman and degrading treatment and not as acts constituting torture. The Commission itself has consistently considered that being beaten and receiving “thrashings” constitutes a general violation of Article 5 of the African Charter.

The United Nations Human Rights Committee confirms this position in its decision Mulezi v. DRC by considering that the fact that the Complainant was beaten constitutes a general violation of the relevant provisions of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. However, both the provisions of the Covenant and the Committee's interpretation concur in apprehending torture not as the acts complained of in themselves but rather as the legal characterisation of an event or conduct on the basis of their holistic and contextual evaluation.

Thus, while recalling the Covenant's silence as to the definition of torture, the Committee observes that the distinction between inhuman treatment and torture is to be sought in the nature, purpose and severity of the treatment inflicted. With particular regard to torture, the Committee emphasises, in its General Comment No. 20, that the incriminated acts must cause atrocious suffering intentionally inflicted, have the purpose of obtaining information or confessions, of punishing the victim for real or alleged acts, and be attributable to a State official or a person acting in that capacity. The Commission adopts this nomenclature in its decision Sudan Human Rights Organisation and Another v. Sudan.

On the assessment of acts constituting torture, the Commission adopts a consistent jurisprudential position as shown by its decisions in the cases of Malawi African Association and Others v. Mauritania and Achuthan and Amnesty International v. Malawi cited above. In those precedents, the Commission concluded that being buried and burned constituted torture. In the same cases, the deliberate refusal by police officers to grant victims access to health care had been considered an act of torture. Moreover, in the Robben Island Guidelines on Torture in Africa, the Commission emphasises the imperative of a minimum of guarantees for persons deprived of their liberty including, among others, the right to an examination by an independent doctor and appropriate medical care.

In the light of the foregoing, the Commission recalls that the prohibition of torture is peremptory. In this regard, the Commission observes that the provisions of Article 5 of the African Charter, even if they do not expressly indicate the universal and peremptory character of the prohibition of torture, do contain its spirit. In the view of the Commission, it cannot be otherwise, since this prohibition has passed into customary international law and even situations of lawful detention, state of emergency or armed conflict cannot justify derogating from it. The United Nations adopts the same position in its Body of Principles for the Protection of All Persons under Any Form of Detention or Imprisonment by providing that no circumstance may be invoked to justify torture or inhuman treatment.

In the present case, the Commission is of the view that the fact that the victims were beaten would no doubt have constituted only inhuman treatment had the acts complained of not reached a certain threshold of cruelty. The victims were indeed beaten until death ensued in the case of at least some of them. It thus appears that, having been held in public detention centres and accused of acts of secession, the victims were inflicted the most atrocious sufferings. Photographs and extracts from consultation registers indicate, for example, that one of the victims had his toes torn off while another was shot in the abdomen to confirm the rumour that this victim had the gift of resisting firearms.

Moreover, the Commission notes that the Respondent State, despite its assurances on this point, was unable to produce proof, in particular by certificate, that the victims concerned remained in their physical and moral integrity throughout their detention. The mere existence of relevant legislation and of court decisions convicting State agents cannot constitute proof that torture has been banished from the practices of law enforcement officers in the territory of the Respondent State. It must still be proved that the victims were able to benefit from the protective environment that national legislation guarantees, which is lacking in the present case.

Furthermore, as decided by the Commission in the case of Law Office of Ghazi Suleiman v. Sudan I, it is the duty of the State, in cases of inhuman treatment, to take measures proportionate to the cruelty of the alleged acts. It appears that, despite having been amply informed of the allegations of torture, at least upon notification of the Complaint submitted before the Commission, the Respondent State was unable to prove that it had initiated investigative measures to respond to them. Finally, the mere fact that the acts imputed to the victims caused material damage and the death of a public official cannot, contrary to what the Respondent State suggests, authorise absolute discretion as to the choice of methods of investigation.

Likewise, the Commission is of the view that the presence of an infirmary within the place of detention cannot, by itself, suffice to guarantee detained persons the right of access to appropriate medical care. In the present Communication, in response to the Complainant's allegations on this point, the State was unable to prove that the victims actually had access to the care offered by the health structure installed within the prison. From the arguments invoked by the Complainant, it appears that the impossibility of having the victims examined in order to establish medical certificates to support the allegations of torture clearly proves a lack of access to health care. Such a lack is attributable to the Respondent State, the victims being detained in a public institution. In such circumstances, the Commission finds that the right of the Complainants to access medical care during their detention was not respected.

The facts thus being compared with the provisions of the African Charter and the relevant jurisprudence, it falls to the Commission to find that the alleged facts constitute inhuman acts and torture. The Commission concludes that the provisions of Article 5 of the Charter have been violated.

From the arguments developed by the Parties on the merits, it emerges that the allegations of violation of Article 7 of the African Charter concern the jurisdiction of the trial court, the right to defence and the right to be tried within a reasonable time and by an impartial court. In the examination of these successive points, the Commission's analysis will focus essentially on the questions in dispute concerning the alleged violations of the provisions of Articles 7(1)(a), 7(1)(c) and 7(1)(d) of the African Charter.

To begin with the competence of the Military Tribunal of Yaoundé, the Commission notes that the Respondent State alleges both the material and the local competence of the said court, on the basis of legislative and regulatory acts. In sum, new legislation amending the ordinance in force on the judicial organisation of the State divested ordinary law courts as of right of offences concerning weapons of war in order to give jurisdiction to the Military Tribunal of Yaoundé, with national territorial jurisdiction. It is under the influence of this amendment that the victims, all civilians, were tried by a military tribunal, principally for carrying firearms and possession of ammunition; and, in the alternative, for destruction of public property and homicide.

The Commission is of the view that, even if States Parties to the African Charter have full discretion as to the adoption of national norms, any national legislation must comply with the obligations laid down by the Charter and relevant international law. With particular regard to the personal as well as material jurisdiction of military tribunals, the Commission considers that this is a question of principle whose resolution necessarily refers to a methodical examination of the original functions and purposes of the said courts. Both doctrine and judicial practice agree that military tribunals are disciplinary mechanisms created to hear offences of a military type, provided for by military legislation, committed by members of military personnel and when the latter are subject to military legislation. In sum, and even at the risk of tautology, the competence of military courts is strictly military whether rationae personae or rationae loci.

In the view of the Commission, a peremptory requirement results from this restriction: military courts cannot try civilians. On the question, the United Nations treaty bodies, namely the Human Rights Committee and the Committee against Torture, adopt the same position. Thus and very aptly, in the case of Akwanga v. Cameroon decided in 2011, the Human Rights Committee concluded that military courts cannot, in principle, have personal jurisdiction to try civilians. Referring to its General Comment No. 32, the Committee had concluded that the Republic of Cameroon had failed to prove that the competence of the military tribunal was absolutely justified in the circumstances of the case. It is important to underline that in the case heard by the Committee, the Complainant, Mbongo Akangwa, had also been tried by the same Military Tribunal of Yaoundé, on the same charges of secessionism.

The Commission notes that the regional human rights protection bodies also go in the same direction as the Akwanga jurisprudence while adopting a progressive and more peremptory approach. By way of illustration, the European Court of Human Rights makes a strict separation between the spheres of competence of military tribunals and those of ordinary law. In particular, it emerges from a review of the jurisprudence that the European Court of Human Rights disqualifies military tribunals vested with jurisdiction to try civilians or whose judges are appointed by the Respondent State.

As regards the Inter-American Court of Human Rights, it takes a consistent and unequivocal position. Among the Court's most emblematic judgments on the question, one may cite the cases of Loayza Tamayo v. Peru and Rosendo Radilla v. Mexico. In the first case, the prohibition is justified by the lack of independence and impartiality inherent in military courts. In the second, the regional court decided that “in a democratic State governed by the rule of law, the criminal military jurisdiction shall have a restrictive and exceptional scope and shall be directed toward the protection of special juridical interests, related to the functions assigned by law to the military forces”.

The Commission itself has without any doubt adopted the strictest position as to the prohibition on military courts exercising jurisdiction over civilians. This stance has manifested itself both through jurisprudential edicts and on the occasion of the examination of States' reports.

As regards jurisprudence, the Commission has adopted a peremptory and consistent approach. Thus, in its landmark decision Law Office of Ghazi Suleiman v. Sudan, the Commission admits no exception to the personal jurisdiction of military tribunals “whose mission is to hear offences of a purely military nature committed by strictly military personnel”. Such a jurisprudential position was based, among other things, on the fact that the composition, hierarchical relations and procedures adopted before military courts cannot provide the minimum guarantees necessary for a fair trial, equality before the law and the independence of the judiciary. Unequivocally, the Commission considers, as it decided for example in the case of Media Rights Agenda v. Nigeria, that the fact of military tribunals trying civilians violates the provisions of Article 7 of the African Charter.

In line with this jurisprudential position, the Commission has never ceased, on the occasion of the examination of States' reports, to insist on the imperative prohibition of the jurisdiction of military tribunals over civilians. For example, in its Concluding Observations following the examination of the Periodic Reports of Uganda in 2006 and 2009, the Commission urgently called on the State under review to expressly proscribe in its legislation the trial of civilians by military courts. The Commission's call followed the refusal of the Government of Uganda to enforce the decisions of the Constitutional Court and the Supreme Court which had declared, in violation of the Constitution, the trial by the Court Martial of Karamojong civilian farmer-herders for terrorist activity and use of weapons.

In the present case, the Commission finds that the Respondent State legally provided for and authorised the trial of the victims by the Military Tribunal of Yaoundé. In the light of the jurisprudence thus recalled, such an authorisation manifestly violates the relevant international law to which the Republic of Cameroon is a party, in particular the provisions of Article 7(1)(a) of the African Charter.

With regard to the allegation of violation of the right to defence protected by Article 7(1)(c) of the African Charter, the Commission recalls that it is a fundamental obligation for courts to communicate with the accused in a language he understands, throughout the proceedings. The argument based on the constitutional obligation for every Cameroonian citizen to understand English and French cannot therefore succeed. Referring to its Principles and Guidelines on the Right to a Fair Trial, the Commission notes that the duty incumbent on the State in this matter is to provide the accused person with translation and interpretation services in the language he understands. In the present case, the victims were all English-speaking and complained of having been questioned in French.

In this regard, the Respondent State refers to the 24th docket of judgment No. 230/99 of 5 October 1999 to prove that the victims did have the right to the assistance of two interpreters. This allegation is not refuted by the Complainant who rather raises the application of two procedures, one adversarial and the other inquisitorial, without however succeeding in countering the assignment of interpreters proved by the Respondent State. The argument invoked by the Complainant on this specific point not having been sufficiently supported, the Commission cannot conclude that there was a violation of Article 7(1)(c) of the African Charter.

Finally, the Complainant alleges the violation of the right protected by Article 7(1)(d), to be tried within a reasonable time by an impartial court. On the arguments based on this violation, the Commission recalls that, without giving a specific definition of the notion of reasonable time, it has consistently assessed the reasonable time of domestic proceedings according to the circumstances of each case, thus on a case-by-case basis. Thus, the Commission has held as unduly long proceedings that lasted ten, five and two years, on the basis in particular of the requirements of the domestic law of the Respondent State, the conduct of the authorities and of the Complainant, the facts of the case and the particular situation of the Complainants.

On the question of the attribution to the Respondent State of the unduly long duration of domestic proceedings, the Commission has consistently concluded that particular surmountable circumstances cannot be invoked to justify a delay manifestly prejudicial to the rights of the litigant. For example, the Commission decided in the case of Pagnoule (on behalf of Mazou) v. Cameroon, that a trial that lasted two years without the slightest procedural act having been carried out by the Supreme Court violates the right to be tried within a reasonable time. The Commission carries out a more in-depth examination of the question in the decision Article 19 v. Eritrea where it considers that neither the seriousness or complexity of the alleged crimes, nor the congestion of the trial court's docket, nor the political situation within the Respondent State can justify a derogation from the right to be tried within a reasonable time.

In the present case, the Commission notes that the Respondent State does not contest that the Court of Appeal incurred a delay by examining the victims' application only nearly seven years after its submission. However, the State's defence is based mainly on the failure of the President of the Republic to appoint some of the judges who were to sit in the composition of the appellate court.

In this regard, the Commission observes that according to the general principle of equity and justice, delay incurred in proceedings before domestic courts is attributable as of right to the State. Such a delay cannot therefore prejudice litigants. In the view of the Commission, there is no doubt that the fact that the Respondent State took more than five years to make appointments had a direct impact on the time within which the victims were to have their fate settled. Indeed, the appellants could, for example, have been released if the Court of Appeal had examined their appeal within a reasonable time.

On this same point, the Commission notes that the situation did not improve in the subsequent course of the domestic proceedings, in particular concerning the appeal still pending before the Supreme Court. Indeed, more than five years have elapsed after the appeal on points of law without the slightest act or decision having been taken. Consequently, the violations suffered since the decision of the Military Tribunal were aggravated by the Respondent State since the victims were denied the right to challenge a decision manifestly contrary to the international obligations of the Republic of Cameroon. The victims were thus forced to serve sentences even though the proceedings were prolonged indefinitely. The Commission considers that such a situation would amount to paralysing existing legal remedies with the potential aim of having sentences imposed in violation of international human rights law served. In these circumstances, justice could not be rendered within a reasonable time as prescribed by the relevant provisions of Article 7(1)(d).

On the alleged violation of the right to be tried by an impartial court, the Commission notes that it has already found the peremptory character of the prohibition on military courts trying civilians. In the leading jurisprudence, the Commission has consistently concluded that such a prohibition is based mainly on the lack of impartiality and independence inherent in military tribunals when they have jurisdiction to try civilians. Moreover, and without needing to dwell any further on the subsequent arguments, the Commission finds that the provisions of Article 7(1)(d) of the African Charter have not been complied with.

In addition to a decision concluding that the provisions of Articles 5 and 7 of the African Charter were violated, the Complainant requests the Commission to order the Republic of Cameroon to pay the total sum of 3,000,000,000 (three billion) CFA francs to all eighteen victims.

Having concluded that the provisions of Articles 5, 7(1)(a) and 7(1)(d) of the African Charter were violated, the Commission must rule on the request for reparation made by the Complainant. The Commission recognises the inherent principle of the right to reparation for the harm suffered as a result of a violation of the provisions of the African Charter. The Commission is of the view that follow-up must be given to the request for monetary compensation when the Complainant or the victims make one, as is the case in the present case. The Commission further recalls that, in the light of its jurisprudence, the assessment of the quantum of such compensation is left to the courts or national authorities of the Respondent State.

However, the Commission observes that the discretion of the competent authorities of the Respondent State as to the assessment of the quantum of reparations must be exercised in compliance with the minimum standards accepted at the international level. Thus, any assessment must be guided by the principle of restitutio in integrum, that is, to place the victim in the position prior to the violation as far as possible. In cases where restitution is impossible, the Respondent State may resort separately or cumulatively to compensation, rehabilitation and other modes of reparation. In the event of disappearance or death, reparation must go to the benefit of the victim's beneficiaries. Finally, any reparation must be just, adequate, effective, sufficient, appropriate, victim-oriented and proportionate to the harm suffered.

The Commission notes that the Parties agree that the initial sentences imposed on the victims by the Military Tribunal of Yaoundé in 1999 range from eight (08) to twenty (20) years' imprisonment and life imprisonment. From the information submitted by the Parties, it emerges that the total duration of detention exceeded the quantum of the sentences imposed by the first court for several of the victims. The victims sentenced to sentences shorter than the total duration of detention consequently had to be released after having served the sentence, since the proceedings were prolonged. On the other hand, the victims sentenced to longer sentences should still be in detention.

On the basis of the preceding findings, the Commission considers that with regard to the acts of torture and inhuman treatment, pecuniary reparation is both appropriate and indispensable to heal the victims' wounds. As regards the violation of the provisions of 7(1)(a) and 7(1)(d), the Commission notes that at the date of the Complaint in 2004, the victims had already been detained for seven years while their appeal was left pending owing to the inaction of the authorities of the Respondent State.

That said, the detention having continued during the proceedings before the Supreme Court, a consequent computation must follow, in particular for the persons still detained at the date of the present decision. Indeed, at the date of its decision, the Commission had received from the Respondent State no indication that the Supreme Court had deliberated. In any event, the jurisdiction attributed to the Military Tribunal of Yaoundé to try the victims not being in conformity with the international obligations of the Respondent State, the sentences imposed by the said court are affected by the same lack of conformity.

As a consequence of the violations found and in application of the principles of equity and justice, adequate and sufficient compensation is required for the persons who have served all or part of the initial sentence. As regards the persons still in detention, given the non-conformity of the Military Tribunal's judgment with the African Charter and the time of suffering and deprivation of liberty already endured in the conditions found by the Commission, an outright release is required in addition.

The Commission notes that under the provisions of Rule 112(2) of its Rules of Procedure, when the decision has been rendered against a Respondent State, the parties must, within a period of one hundred and eighty (180) days from notification of the decision, inform the Commission in writing of any measures taken or being taken by the Respondent State to give effect to the decision. The Commission, For these reasons,
Finds that the Republic of Cameroon did not violate the provisions of Article 7(1)(c) of the African Charter.

Declares, on the other hand, that the Republic of Cameroon violated the provisions of Articles 5, 7(1)(a) and 7(1)(d) of the African Charter. Consequently: i. Urges the Republic of Cameroon to take the necessary measures for the immediate and outright release of all persons still in detention. ii. Further requests the Republic of Cameroon to pay all the victims or their beneficiaries appropriate, just and adequate compensation. The amount of compensation shall be calculated taking into account the pretium doloris on account of the acts of torture and inhuman treatment, the harm suffered on account of the detention, the duration of the proceedings and the expenses incurred. iii. Strongly recommends that the Republic of Cameroon take the necessary measures to punish those responsible for the acts of torture and inhuman treatment suffered by the victims. iv. Further recommends that the Republic of Cameroon ensure within its competent institutions, particularly law enforcement institutions and places of detention, a better knowledge and strict application of the relevant international law and national legislation on torture and cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment. v. Urgently recommends that the Republic of Cameroon bring its legislation on judicial organisation into conformity with the African Charter and its international human rights obligations by restoring full and exclusive jurisdiction to ordinary law courts to try civilians. vi. Finally requests the Republic of Cameroon to report to it in writing, within one hundred and eighty (180) days of notification of the present decision, on the measures taken to implement these recommendations. Adopted at the 15th Extraordinary Session of the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights, held from 7 to 14 March 2014, in Banjul, The Gambia.

This Communication was received at the Secretariat of the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights (“the Secretariat,” and “the Commission”) on 10 December 2009. It is submitted by Mohammed Abdullah Saleh Al-Asad (the Complainant) through the Global Justice Clinic (previously the ‘International Human Rights Clinic (IHRC)’) of the Centre for Human Rights and Global Justice, Washington Square Legal Services Inc, New York University School of Law; and the International Centre for the Legal Protection of Human Rights (INTERIGHTS), (hereinafter jointly referred to as ‘Representatives’).

The Communication is submitted against the Republic of Djibouti, a Party to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights (‘the Charter’) since 20 December, 1991 and bound by its provisions since 20 March 1992 in terms of Article 65 of the Charter.

The Complainant states that he is a citizen of Yemen. From 1985 until 2003 he lived in the Republic of Tanzania and established a family there. He also had a successful business. To facilitate his residence and business undertakings including acquisition of land in Tanzania, he obtained a forged Tanzanian birth certificate and a passport.

He states that on 26 December, 2003 around 9:00 pm while at his home in Dar es Salaam, two men who spoke the Swahili language and appeared to him to be Tanzanians apprehended and blindfolded him; bound his hands; and abruptly took him to an apartment where he was questioned for about five hours concerning his entry and residence in Tanzania and how he obtained a Tanzanian passport.

In the early hours of 27 December, 2003 he was once again handcuffed, blindfolded, and taken to the airport where he was put on a small aircraft and flown to an undisclosed destination. The Tanzanian authorities did not inform the Complainant or his family and friends about the reason for his apprehension or indeed his whereabouts. The flight took a few several hours. Upon landing, the Complainant was quickly pushed into a motor vehicle and driven for about half an hour to a detention facility where he was kept in isolation for two weeks.

During the second week he was interrogated about three times concerning terrorist-related activities. The interrogations centred on his relationship with certain terrorist suspects, and Al-Haramain, an Islamic Foundation to which had previously rented office premises in his property in Tanzania and of which he had been appointed as a co-trustee. The interrogations were carried out in English with the help of an Arabic language interpreter. He denied involvement in any terrorist- related activities.

Concerning the conditions of his detention, the Complainant states that he was first briefly kept in a small old dirty and unfurnished room, and then transferred to a bigger and cleaner room which only had an old sponge mattress, a toilet, a tap, and a plastic basin. After a few days he was provided with a pillow and a sheet. He was never allowed a change of clothes for the entire two weeks. High up the walls of the room were two small windows which opened to the outside. Another window was on the iron door. During the night, there were a lot of mosquitoes which prevented him from sleeping. From this cell, he could hear motor vehicles passing by, the call to prayer, and children playing, all which gave him the impression that he was in a residential area.

The Complainant states that at the end of the two weeks, he was once more bound, blindfolded, and driven from the secret detention facility to an airport ‘by local personnel’. He further alleges that at the airport, he was pulled from the car, lifted off the ground and his blindfold was ripped off. He saw about five individuals clad in black with their faces concealed with balaclavas. The men tore off his clothing, shoved a finger into his rectum, photographed him naked, diapered him, and dressed him in a short sleeved shirt and a pair of trousers. Further, they plugged his ears with cotton, placed headphones and a hood over his head, tightly taped around his head, while his hands, waist, and feet were chained. He was then put on a waiting plane and flown out in turn to three detention facilities allegedly operated by the United States of America, two of which were in Afghanistan.

He states that in the subsequent secret detention facilities, he was still never allowed contact with the outside world including his own family and friends, organisations, and legal counsel. In addition he was subjected to continued isolate detention, constant loud music, dietary manipulation, artificial light twenty-four hours a day, and exposed to cold weather.

Eventually on 5 May 2005, he was transferred by the United States Government to Yemen where he was subsequently tried for forging travel documents, convicted upon his own plea of guilt, sentenced to time served, and released on 14 March 2006. He was and has never been charged with any terrorism-related offences.

Whereas at first the Complainant had no knowledge of the first destination from Tanzania and the location of his detention, he believes that it was in the territory of the Republic of Djibouti. His belief is premised on a set of circumstantial evidence collated from his own experiences and observations whilst in his first secret detention facility outside Tanzania; documents filed with the High Court of Tanzania on a habeas corpus application filed by his father; expert testimony; and various reports of international organisations and the mass media documenting the United States of America’s extraordinary rendition program undertaken as part of the counter-terrorism measures from the immediate aftermath of the terrorist attack of 11 September 2001 in the United States of America.

The Complainant further alleges that he believes the agents of the Government of Djibouti were involved from the moment of his arrival allegedly in Djibouti to the time he was handed over to the US agents who continued to detain and severally transfer him to the three subsequent secret detention facilities.

On 31 March 2009 his lawyers wrote the Attorney General of the Respondent State detailing the facts of his experiences during his secret detention by way of notice of violations of his rights as guaranteed under the African Charter.

The Complainant alleges that despite the notice, the Respondent State has not undertaken an effective investigation to discover additional information regarding his alleged detention and treatment in Djibouti. He further states that the Respondent State has neither identified and prosecuted those responsible, nor offered any other form of remedy to him.
The Complainant avers that the treatment he suffered at the alleged instance of the Respondent State amount to violations of Articles 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7(1), 12(4), 14, and 18 of the Charter.

Consequent upon the alleged violations the Complainant requests the Commission to:- (a) Recommend that the Republic of Djibouti should award him due compensation. (b) Recommend that the Republic of Djibouti should conduct a public inquiry into illegal apprehensions, renditions, and detentions in the context of counter- terrorism measures such as those exacted on him. (c) Require the Republic of Djibouti to report to the African Commission within six months on:- (i) the steps taken to investigate and prosecute any person responsible for the violation of his rights. (ii) the measures adopted to ensure appropriate oversight of foreign military and intelligence services on its territory as a guarantee for non-repetition of the type of violations he suffered.

On 7 October 2013 the Secretariat wrote the named expert witness inviting him to attend at the oral hearing. The Respondent State was duly informed of Mr Sifton’s attendance and role during the oral hearing by a Note Verbale dated 7 October 2013 referenced? ACHPR/COMM/DJI/383/10/1021/13.
The Secretariat subsequently received the full list of persons that would be appearing for the Respondent State and the Complainant by their respective letters of 11 and 16 October 2013 respectively.

On 25 October 2013 the Secretariat further received from the Respondent State Observations of the Republic of Djibouti on Complainant’s Final Response on Admissibility and New Facts, attaching two exhibits being a Picture of Aircraft Registration No 5H-TZE from Tanzania Civil Aviation Authority, and the Republic of Djibouti’s Code de Procedure Penale.
The oral hearing was eventually held on 2 November 2013 during the 54 Ordinary Session held from 22 October to 5 November 2013.

By a letter dated 4 November 2013 which was after the oral hearing but before the 54 Ordinary Session was concluded, the Complainant purported to file further observations on admissibility in response to the Respondent State’s submissions during the oral hearing. The Complainant’s post-hearing observations attached a further document being the Declaration of Mr. Sam Raphael with eight exhibits.

The Commission consider the propriety of the Complainant’s post-hearing written observations and declined to have recourse to them for purposes of its decision on admissibility as this amounted to reopening arguments which had been closed upon the oral hearing. The Complainant was informed accordingly by letter dated 15 November 2013 referenced ACHPR/COMM/383/10/DJI/1274/13.

Lastly, on 20 November 2013 the Respondent State wrote the Commission objecting to the further submissions purported to be filed by the Complainant on 4 November 2013. The Respondent State went further to make its own observations on the Complainant’s post-hearing submissions. The Commission declined to consider the Respondent State’s post-hearing observations for the same reasons stated at paragraph 51 above. Objections on procedure and the Commission’s decision Complainant’s Objections to the Respondent State’s additional written arguments

In what was intended to be his last submissions on admissibility, the Complainant objects to the Respondent State’s Reply on Admissibility. The Complainant contends that the Respondent State’s Reply on Admissibility amounts to an abuse of process and is contrary to Rule 105 of Rules of Procedure. Accordingly he prays that the Reply and the supporting evidence must be disregarded by the Commission in arriving at its decision on admissibility. Respondent State’s Submission on the Complainant’s Objection

For its part, the Respondent State addresses the Complainant’s objection in its ‘Observations on the Complainant’s Final Response on Admissibility and New Facts’ which was yet another written submission. The Respondent State observes that its Reply on Admissibility was specifically allowed upon request by the Commission. Accordingly the Respondent State maintains that it’s Reply on Admissibility and the supporting affidavits should not and cannot be disregarded. The African Commission’s Analysis and Decision on the Objections

The African Commission would like to observe that the procedure adopted in this Communication with respect to parties’ written arguments represents an extremely exceptional departure from its Rules of Procedure, in particular Rule 105.

Rule 105 (2) and (3) of the Rules of Procedure provides for the parties to submit a total of three written submissions starting with the Complainant’s arguments on admissibility, followed by the Respondent State’s arguments on admissibility, and ending with the Complainant’s comments on the Respondent State’s written arguments. These are provided for with strict deadlines, subject to a single possible extension not exceeding one month in terms of Rule 113 of the Rules of Procedure.
In accordance with Rule 105 (4), any further observations may only be presented at an oral hearing as may be allowed by the African Commission under Rule 88(6) of the Rules of Procedure.

The African Commission would like to affirm that it does not espouse a relaxed approach in the application of its Rules of Procedure. Among the objects of its Rules of Procedure regarding Communications generally and submission of written arguments in particular is to ensure that parties are accorded equal, fair and adequate opportunity to present their respective positions, and that alleged violations or any matters that are in contention between the parties are clearly identified and determined expeditiously and conclusively.

Whereas the Rules of Procedure constitute a comprehensive code designed to achieve among others, the above objects, the Commission retains the prerogative to permit or require further written submissions outside the strict stipulations in the Rules of Procedure and in place of an oral hearing. However, the Commission would only do so in extremely exceptional circumstances in respect of which it does not even find it desirable to enunciate criteria. For all purposes, parties are well advised to strictly adhere to the provisions of its Rules of Procedure. The Commission will not hesitate to impose necessary procedural sanctions for default such as declining to consider a given submission that does not comply with the Rules of Procedure and acceptable practice.

In the present Communication, the Commission indeed allowed the Respondent State to file its Reply on Admissibility by way of observations on the Complainant’s Response to the State’s Arguments on Admissibility. The Commission considered, among others, that the Complainant’s own second observations are more voluminous than his initial arguments on admissibility, in the process raising multiple new points, introducing three new expert declarations, and citing various new sources in support of the observations.

In addition, it is the Complainant’s own manner of submitting arguments and supporting evidence that partly led to the escalation of written submissions for both parties. Among others, the Complainant omitted to attach some critical evidence to his initial arguments on admissibility and only provided the relevant evidence upon being prompted by the Commission. By the time the Complainant submitted the omitted evidence, the Respondent State had already filed its Arguments on Admissibility. This led the Commission to transmit the Complainant’s missing evidence to the Respondent State with a request to submit its observations thereon which ordinarily would have been canvassed in the Respondent State’s initial arguments. The Respondent State’s observations on the omitted documents are contained in its Supplemental Arguments.

Further, whereas close to a year elapsed between the time the Complainant’s Arguments on Admissibility were received by the Secretariat and the time the Respondent State filed its arguments on admissibility, the Complainant subsequently also took about four months to submit his observations, contrary to the one month allowed under Rule 105(3) of the Rules of Procedure. As noted above, even when the Complainant eventually submitted, he then introduced substantial new points and supporting materials, a trend which continued for both parties until after the oral hearing.

Even more, subsequent to the contested Respondent State’s Reply, both parties submitted further observations making the total number of written exchanges escalate to eleven with the very last two having been rejected by the Commission for being an abuse of process.
At all times the Commission endeavoured to avert the possibility of an oral hearing. As it turned out, however, an oral hearing was still held.

The Commission is satisfied that considering the intricacy and relevance of the matters contested in the present Communication, both parties were unprecedentedly and unusually accorded more than ample, equal and fair opportunity to present their respective positions culminating in the oral hearing held during the 54 Ordinary Session.

Accordingly, although the Complainant’s objection is prima facie valid in terms of Rule 105 of the Rules of Procedure, the Commission confirms that it has, as a measure of exception, allowed the Respondent State’s Reply.
