In addressing the exceptions to Article 56(5) the Respondent State argues that the question now is whether the Complainants' case falls within the exception to Article 56(5) to warrant the African Commission to waive compliance with this mandatory requirement. It submits that the Complainants' case does not fall within the exceptions for the following reasons - that: • Ample local remedies are available to victims who allege violation of their rights, including civil mechanisms up to the Supreme Court of Nigeria; • There are other additional mechanisms for redress, such as the National Human Rights Commission, Public Complaints Commission, Federal Character Commission, Code of Conduct Bureau, Citizens' Rights Department of the Federal Ministry of Justice and Legal Aid Council; • In criminal cases, victims can lodge a complaint before the law enforcement authorities - the police; • The Government of Nigeria has instituted a reform agenda to overhaul the entire criminal justice administration; • There are "writs of mandamus" and "habeas corpus" orders which can be sought from courts against the decisions of police authorities; • The allegations of harassment, arbitrary arrest and purported assassinations are spurious allegations that are unfounded; and hence the Complainant is yet to exhaust local remedies.
The African Commission has examined the Complaint and the submissions of both parties under Article 56 of the African Charter.

While the submissions of the Respondent State on Admissibility do not appear to challenge the Complainant under sub-Articles 1, 2, 3, 6, 7 of Article 56, the parties' submissions are at variance under sub-Articles 4 and 5.

Under sub-article 4, the Respondent State claims that the Complaint is exclusively based on media reports of allegations of violations of human rights. The Complainant, on the other hand, avers that while its Complaint makes considerable references to media sources, it was not filed on the strength of information derived from media sources alone as it includes cases with respect to which the Complainant carried out its own investigations and with respect to which it made legal representations to the relevant authorities on behalf of the families of the victims.

In examining Article 56(4), the Commission relies on its jurisprudence wherein it dealt with similar cases. In Communication 147/95 and 149/96 Sir Dawda K Jawara/The Gambia, the Commission had held that "while it would be dangerous to rely exclusively on news disseminated from the mass media, it would be equally damaging if the Commission were to reject a Communication because some aspects of it are based on news disseminated through the mass media. This is borne out of the fact that the Charter makes use of the word 'exclusively.'" It went on to add: There is no doubt that the media remains the most important, if not the only source of information. It is common knowledge that information on human rights violations is always gotten from the media. The genocide in Rwanda, the human rights abuses in Burundi, Zaire, Congo, to name but a few, were revealed by the media. The issue therefore should not be whether the information was gotten from the media, but whether the information is correct. Did the complainant try to verify the truth about these allegations? Did he have the means or was it possible for him to do so, given the circumstances of his case?

The Commission has taken a careful look at the submissions from the Complainant. While it has admitted that some of the allegations draw upon media reports, most of the information contained therein cannot be said to be based exclusively on news disseminated through the mass media. For one thing, the Complainant has indicated that on occasions, it did its own research in ascertaining the facts, which the Respondent State has not denied in its entirety. The Complainant alleges extra-judicial execution and has enumerated a number of such cases in its submissions. The Respondent State, on the other hand, while claiming that the Complaint relied on news reports, still admitted that there were indeed instances of extra-judicial killings in the country which it said its authorities continue to deal with.

Reading through the Complaint, it is clear that that the Communication is not based exclusively on news disseminated through the mass media, but rather on primary information provided by the Respondent State itself, the Complainant's research and an exhaustive list of names and addresses as provided by the Complainant, which has not been denied by the Respondent State. The African Commission, thus, is of the view that the claim that the Complainant's allegations as filed before the African Commission are exclusively based on news report cannot be sustained. Accordingly, the Commission rules that the Communication complies with Article 56(4) of the African Charter.

The core of contention of the two parties on the issue of Admissibility lies over the requirement of exhaustion of local remedies as stipulated under Article 56(5) of the African Charter. This provision provides that Communications should be 'sent after exhausting local remedies, if any, unless it is obvious that this procedure is unduly prolonged'.

In human rights law it is supremely important for a person whose rights have been violated to make use of domestic remedies to right the wrong, rather than address the issue to an international body. The rule of exhaustion of local remedies is widely recognized by the major international human rights treaties. For instance, the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and its Optional Protocol I, the European Convention on the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms and the American Convention on Human Rights all recognize the principle of exhaustion of local remedies. Similarly, the African Charter, as indicated above, has a provision that deals with exhaustion of local remedies. The rule is founded on the premise that the full and effective implementation of international obligations in the field of human rights is designed to enhance the enjoyment of human rights and fundamental freedoms at the national level and this is supplemented by the fact that "local remedies are normally quicker, cheaper, and more effective than international ones."

The rationale, therefore, behind the exhaustion of local remedies rule is that a state should be given the opportunity to address the issue before the matter is brought before international treaty bodies. In the African human rights system, the Commission has confirmed and reconfirmed this position in its decisions. For example in Free Legal Assistance Group and Others v Zaire and Recontre Africaine pour la Defense des Droits de l'Homme v Zambia, the African Commission stated that the requirement of exhaustion of local remedies is founded on the principle that a government should have notice of human rights violation in order to have the opportunity to remedy such violations before being called before an international body. This provision also enables the African Commission to avoid playing the role of a court of first instance, a role that it cannot under any circumstances arrogate to itself.
The Commission will now proceed to examine and evaluate the submissions of the parties in relation to Article 56 (5).

The Complainant agrees that the exhaustion of local remedies is a condition precedent to bringing a Complaint before the African Commission. It further agrees that exhausting local remedies is a recognized principle in international law, with the objective of giving domestic courts an opportunity to decide upon a matter before that matter is brought before an international forum. It also agrees that exhausting local remedies notifies the government of the wrongs it is being accused of, in order to give it the opportunity to remedy those wrongs within its own judicial system.

The Complainant however argues that in the present Communication an exception to the exhaustion of domestic remedies rule would apply if the local remedies are unavailable, inadequate or ineffective. It argues that the Complaint constitutes a compelling exception to the requirement of exhaustion of local remedies and requests the Commission to waive this requirement as demonstrated in its jurisprudence. In rebutting the allegations and arguments of the Complainant, the Respondent State avers that the exhaustion of the local remedy rule is a fundamental requirement that must be met and can and shall only be waived under very limited circumstances. It calls upon the Commission not to admit what it describes as 'spurious claims that cannot be substantiated.' It further argues that ample and effective local remedies are available to victims who allege violation of their rights, including civil mechanisms up to the Supreme Court of Nigeria.

The Commission has always held the view that the initial burden is on the Complainant to prove that they have met the requirement set out in Article 56 (5) of the African Charter. Thereafter, the burden shifts to the Respondent State, if it contests the Complainant's allegations that remedies are available, effective and sufficient. The Commission has unequivocally held that when a Government "argues that the Communication must be declared inadmissible because local remedies have not been exhausted, the Government then has the burden of demonstrating the existence of such remedies." The onus is thus on the Respondent State, to demonstrate that local remedies are available, sufficient and effective.

As has been stated supra, though the rationale of the rule is to allow the state concerned an opportunity to remedy a grievance through its own domestic legal system, the Commission has stated that will not hold this requirement to apply literally in cases where it is impracticable or undesirable for the Complainant to seize the domestic courts. Accordingly, the African Commission in Dawda Jawara v The Gambia, stated that for a Complainant to be able to exhaust local remedies, such remedies must meet three basic criteria – they must be available, effective and sufficient.

It is instructive to note that the Commission also went on to state in the Jawara case that, if the availability of a remedy is not evident it 'cannot be invoked by the state to the detriment of the Complainant.' In the instant matter, the burden of proof, therefore, falls on the Respondent State to prove that effective local remedies exist and that they are reasonably accessible, available, effective and sufficient. The Commission notes that while there are structures and mechanisms for the redress of violations in territory of the Respondent State, it has not demonstrated through concrete examples of successful prosecutions of errant officers, which it has admitted do exist. It has also not demonstrated to the Commission steps it has taken to address the numerous concerns of the Complainant. For example, in Exhibit G2, the Complainant wrote to the Director of Public Prosecutions, Mrs Bola Ighile on 19 September 2008 concerning the 'Coroners verdict on the killings of Messrs Celestine Chiteo Okoro and Richard Okoroafor and the duty of identifying and prosecuting policemen responsible for the deaths.' In that exhibit the Complainant enclosed a copy of the Coroners verdict on the cause and circumstances surrounding the deaths of the victims. The letter stated that a verdict was delivered on 14 July 2003 after several months of inquiry. It also stated that the Coroner identified the police as responsible for the unlawful killings.

Unfortunately, the letter states, "our efforts and other efforts to get the police to investigate the killings were not fruitful. We could not escape the impression that there was an insufficient disposition to our quest, or a deliberate scheme to either forestall proper investigation into the killings, or wear out, by delay antics, the victims' families resolve to pursue their quest for justice." Consequently, the Complainants initiated coronial processes before the Magistrate sitting at Yaba. It informs the Commission that throughout the inquest sittings, the police authorities made only one appearance, but only to inform the Coroner that a report of the killings which had been submitted to the Commissioner of Police, Lagos State would be made available to her during the inquest. It says no official report was subsequently submitted to the Coroner.

In the view of the Commission the Respondent State has the responsibility to prove accessibility, availability and sufficiency and in its opinion has not done so. The Commission agrees with the Complainant that the Respondent State had enough notice and time to adequately address the violations which it stands accused of and it chose not to address the alleged violations adequately.

In Amnesty International v Sudan, Communication Nos. 48/90, 50/91, 89/93; Malawi African Association v Mauritania, Communications 54/91, 61/91, 98/93, 164/93, 196/97, 210/98; and Free Legal Assistance Group v Zaire, Communications 25/89, 47/90, 56/91 and 100/93 the Commission had interpreted the provisions of Article 56(5) in the light of its duty to protect human and people's rights as stipulated in the Charter, and had argued that it does not believe that the exhaustion of local remedies must be applied literally to those cases in which it is "neither practicable nor desirable" for the complainants or the victims to pursue such internal channels of remedy in every case of violation of human rights. Such is the case where there are many victims as in the instant Communication. The gravity of the human rights situation in the country and the great number of victims involved renders the channels of remedy unavailable in practical terms, and, according to the terms of the Charter, their process is "unduly prolonged". In the above cited Communications the Commission also stated that in a situation of grave and massive violations, it may be impossible to give a complete list of names of all the victims.

Importantly, in the present communication, the Respondent State does not entirely deny the allegations made by the Complainant as it also claims that measures are being taken to address the situation. In effect, the Respondent State is not unaware of the serious and massive human rights violations in the country. It has also not denied that the Complainant has taken numerous steps to bring such violations to its notice, including litigating (without any concrete results) on behalf of some of the alleged victims. The African Commission cannot but agree with the Complainant, (in accordance with its earlier decisions on cases of serious and massive violations of human rights that and in view of the vast and varied scope of the violations alleged and the large number of individuals involved) that the present Complaint need not exhaust domestic remedies. To require a literal exhaustion of local remedies would in effect result into maintaining a technicality for the sake of it, with the result of allowing the Respondent State to benefit from its own wrongs. With all the publicity around the case, the Respondent State is well informed of the matter and that has had every opportunity to initiate an investigation, bring the perpetrators to justice and clear its name. The Respondent State chose not to do that.
For these reasons, the African Commission declares the Communication Admissible.

The Complainant states that Nigeria conducted national elections in April 2007, the second since 29 May 1999, leading to the inauguration of a new set of elected representatives on 29 May 2007, following elections that were locally and internationally condemned as gravely flawed. It states that the Nigerian Government is now headed by Alhaji Umaru Musa Yar'Adua, a former Governor who succeeded former President Olusegun Obasanjo and who belongs to the same political party as the former President.

The Complainant alleges that under the previous regime of President Olusegun Obasanjo, similar hopes of a rule-of-law transformation after nearly fifteen years of blistering military rule were touted and believed, but were soon dashed. It states that for eight years under the former regime, Nigeria gravitated towards a near lawless state, with many agencies of Government acting with scant regard for the rule of law. It alleges that impunity surged within security agencies leading to arbitrary deaths through extra-legal killings, with little concern by Government for its obligations under the constitution, and under regional and international human rights treaties it had ratified.

The Complainant alleges violations of Articles 4, 6, and 7 of the African Charter by the Government of Nigeria. It states that since the Communication was filed, grave human rights violations have persisted, and several more Nigerians have lost their lives to extra-judicial, arbitrary and summary executions by law enforcement and state security agents while the Government remain aloof and indifferent to the abuses.

It states that on the 8 June 2005, in the Apo district of Abuja five young male traders and a female student (namely: Ifeanyi Ozor, Chinedu Meniru, Isaac Ekene, Palinus Ogbonna, Anthony Nwokike and Augustina Arebun) had an encounter with some police officers in Abuja, while the policemen were on patrol duty. All six persons, popularly referred to as "Apo six" were brutally and gruesomely murdered in very chilling, cold-blooded circumstances, after which they were branded as "armed robbers."

It states that widespread public protests, during the visit of the United Nations Special Rapporteur on Arbitrary, Summary and Extrajudicial, Killings, Mr. Philip Alston, pressured the Government into setting up a Judicial Commission of Inquiry to investigate the circumstances surrounding the deaths of the Apo six. The Commission of Inquiry found that the victims were not armed robbers as the police had earlier claimed, but innocent civilians. The Complainant alleges that of the six persons killed, one had tried to escape and another one had managed to survive after the first volley of bullets fired on them. The escapee was caught, and murdered immediately, while the other person who had survived was killed (allegedly strangled) on arrival at the police station. The Complainant alleges that no post-mortem was conducted neither was a death certificate completed by a medical doctor before the bodies of the deceased were hastily buried.

It states that after the Commission of Enquiry's Recommendations, the Olusegun Obasanjo Government in a rare and unprecedented act, paid monetary compensation to the relatives of the victims of the killings, and began prosecution of the perpetrators of the killings. The Complainant states that this display of action towards reinforcing values of accountability turned out to be mostly fortuitous, and the Government was never to repeat similar action to other cases of extra-legal killings by law enforcement agencies afterwards.

The Complainant informs the Commission that Mr. Phillip Alston, the United Nations Special Rapporteur on Extra-judicial, Summary and Arbitrary Executions, in his Report of an official Fact-finding visit to Nigeria between 27 June and 8 July 2005, noted that: The Nigerian Police Force put forth various pretext to justify extra-judicial executions. When a victim is killed in custody, an attempted escape may be cited. When the victim is killed before being taken into custody, his status as an armed robber may be cited.

The Complainant alleges that prior to the Apo Six case, there was the case of some Enugu State University students in 2005. It states that six persons (namely: Murphy Opara, Emeka Madubosa, Uchenna Asogwa, Ikechukwu Asogwa, Chemezie Ugwu and Kelechi Chukwu), mostly university students, were arrested at various locations in Enugu State after a bank robbery on the 27 January 2005, between the period March and April 2005 and transferred to the Ogui Police Area Command in Enugu. On 27 April 2005 they were paraded before journalists at the Enugu State Criminal Investigation Division to publicize police success in fighting crime. Photographs of the six suspects in handcuffs were widely published in the press.

It alleges that a few days later, after more than one month in police custody, the police killed all the six suspects, alleging attempts by the victims to escape from custody. It states that the claims of escape were spurious, unfounded and entirely contrived. It avers that nothing showed, from the manner of the shootings, that shots fired were meant to restrain attempts at escape. It also alleges that after the victims were killed, no autopsies were carried out, the families never saw the bodies of the victims, and it is unknown where they were buried. It states that no credible inquiry was conducted into the killing, and no charges have been brought against the police officers who carried out the killings, nor have relatives of the victims been offered any compensation.

The Complainant further alleges that in Abia State, on or about 9 August 2006, the police paraded 12 robbery suspects, including a 12 year old boy, before the media and the general public at the Central Police Station in Umuahia, Abia State. The suspects, some of whom displayed gunshot wounds were alleged to have been arrested after an exchange of gunfire with the police during which four others were killed at Olokobe Ndume community in Umuahia, North Local Government Area of the State.

It states that following the parade during which double barrel guns, pistols and other weapons, as well as an international passport purportedly recovered from the suspects were displayed, the police killed all the suspects and dumped their bodies at the premises of the Federal Medical Centre, Umuahia after obtaining confessional statements from them. The Complainant alleges that the police admitted responsibility for the killing during a press briefing afterwards. The bodies of the suspects were later buried in a mass grave by authorities of the Federal Medical Centre on the 17 August 2006, about a week after they were dumped there, and were already decomposing. It states that the Government failed to carry out any autopsy or investigation.

The Complainant also informs the Commission that as it was preparing to write a report on the alleged 12 robbery suspects, news media carried another police killing - that of Mr Olusegun Openiyi. The Complainant says that Mr Olusegun Openiyi was staff of Celtel Nigeria, one of the leading telecommunications service providers in Nigeria, and was driving his car at about 8.00 p.m. when he was stopped by policemen from Sabo Police Station close to gate leading to the University of Lagos.

It states that, according to the report, Mr. Olusegun Openiyi stopped and there was an argument between him and the policemen after which he drove off. Soon after driving off, the police fired a shot at one of the rear tyres of his car. Thereafter, the police officer reportedly rushed towards the vehicle, pulled open the door and then fired another shot at Mr. Openiyi. It states that he died soon after he was taken to the Military Hospital at Yaba. The Complainant states that the autopsy report from the Lagos State Teaching Hospital revealed the primary cause of death as hypovolemic shock while the secondary cause was lacerated kidney due to penetrating gunshot to the chest.

The Complainant argues that these mentioned cases have been mostly selected, as representative samples, from a much larger portfolio of abusive deaths brought about by law enforcement officers acting under the cover of their state authority. It says that some reports say that deaths resulting from police abuses, and in extra-judicial circumstances, run up to over a thousand each year. It states that many of these cases are however not reported principally because they are perpetrated under cover and records of such killings are not kept.

To substantiate its claims of extra-legal killings, it quotes again the UN Special Rapporteur: "that while armed robbery does plague much of Nigeria, the label of 'armed robber' is often used to justify the jailing and/ or extra-judicial execution of innocent individuals who have come to the attention of the police for reasons ranging from refusal to pay a bribe to insulting or inconveniencing the police."

The Complainant alleges that a number of deaths have also resulted from in-custody torture in police facilities. Such deaths, it argues, usually arise from dehumanizing custodial conditions, or torture and other inhuman and degrading treatment to which detainees are subjected. Citing a Report by AJ titled "Breaking Point – How Torture and Police Cell System Violate Justice in Criminal Investigation Process in Nigeria" published in June 2005, the Complainant recounts the ordeal of a detained man, named Mr. Ifezina who, while in custody and under interrogation in 2004, was reportedly tortured by third degree methods. It states that Ifezina was stripped naked and made to lie face down, his legs were folded upwards at the knees and tied at the ankles, and his arms were raised upwards and tied together at the wrists. It alleges that a pipe or rod, attached at the ends to a rope hanging from ceiling fan hook in the ceiling, was passed between both legs and both arms. He was then raised towards the ceiling by pulling at the loose ends of the rope, until he was suspended in the air in the form of a human bow – a position that caused excruciating pain all over the body but particularly in the shoulders, the spine and the waist.

The Complainant alleges that whilst Ifezina was suffering this pain, the interrogating officer then began to insert and withdraw an unsterilized needle into and out of his penis through the urinary tract, while asking him questions. It states that blood coursed out of Ifezina's genitals in the meanwhile and spattered the floor while he helplessly screamed from pain. The penis which became swollen subsequently oozed and emitted rancid pus. The police, the Complainant alleges, neither treated him nor allowed him to treat himself which led to his eventual death.

The Complainant alleges that this case and many other instances of investigative torture are reported in Breaking Point – hosted on Access to Justice Website, www.accesstojustice-ng.org. Some other accounts of custodial deaths in Nigeria were reported in Human Rights Watch report titled "Rest in Pieces - Police Torture and Deaths in Custody in Nigeria" published in July 2005 (www.hrw.org/reports/2005/nigeria0705).

It maintains that as a signatory to the African Charter, Nigeria is bound to uphold the principles of human rights enshrined in the African Charter by safeguarding the lives of its citizens. This Charter obligation, it avers, has been repeatedly emphasized by international courts as in the case of the Mapiripan Massacre (Columbia). It argues that while still stressing the same treaty obligation, the British House of Lords in the case of Middleton, R v. HM Coroner for West Somersetshire (2002), stated that the duty to protect life imposes two complementary obligations on the state. Firstly, a substantive duty not to take life and to take reasonable preventative measures to protect an individual whose life is at risk. Secondly, an adjectival procedural obligation to investigate deaths where arguably there has been a breach of the substantive obligation. This second aspect, the Complainant argues, requires reasonable, effective and prompt investigation as stated in the European Court of Human Right case of Mentese and others v Turkey.

The Complainant alleges that despite the recurrence of gross human rights abuses in Nigeria, both internal and oversight mechanisms for investigating police misconduct (including extra-judicial killings), and holding police officers accountable for these abuses are too weak, slack and grossly inadequate to curb the culture of impunity in Nigeria. It states that, according to the Phillip Alton's Report: "On paper, the system for investigating police misconduct is impressive. In practice, it is too often a charade. The outcome of the investigations usually seems to justify inaction or to ensure that complaints are dealt with internally through "orderly room hearings" or the like. While police officers are certainly disciplined and some dismissed, the system has rarely worked in cases in which police are accused of extra judicial executions.... The result gives the appearance of a functioning investigative system, while in fact promoting the goal of defacto police impunity."

The Complainant alleges that the internal disciplinary system of the police force is largely undependable and indicts the police force for its systematic failure to bring policemen to justice for abuses they commit. Quoting the Philip Alston Report, it notes: "Indeed the single greatest impediment to bringing police officers to justice for crimes is the Nigeria Police itself. Evidence indicates that it systematically blocks or hampers investigations and allows suspects to flee. In order to break this cycle of impunity, a new investigation and prosecution mechanism is required."

The Complainant further alleges that the Police Service Commission, which exercises constitutional oversight powers over the appointment, discipline and dismissal of policemen, has largely been inert, ineffective, and unable to restrain police abuses. Quoting the Phillip Alston Report, it further noted that "In terms of governmental accountability, the Police Service Commission is charged with police discipline, but has opted to refer all complaints of extra-judicial police killings back to the police for investigation. The Commission's mandate is potentially empowering. But despite efforts by one or two excellent Commissioners, its performance has been dismal and self restraint. Its quarterly report to the President are not published and present a dismal chronicle of rubber-stamping decisions taken by the police, coupled with inaction in relation to pressing concerns. A radical overhaul of its procedures and composition is warranted."

It argues that the above accounts demonstrate that large-scale violations of the right to life, particularly by law enforcement agents are still continuing in Nigeria while the Nigeria Government is failing on all its obligations to respect, protect and safeguard the right to life in Nigeria. It alleges that the Government fails systematically, to conduct effective and impartial investigations into abuses of human lives when they occur; fails to take action to deter perpetrators of these abuses and bring them to justice when they commit serious crimes; and fails to provide effective remedies for the relatives of families of the victims. The failure of the Government, it avers, to take meaningful steps towards reforming the way law enforcement officers execute their responsibilities, including taking action to dis-establish centres notorious for the perpetration of acts of torture, addressing conditions which bring about impunity in the delivery of policing services, all contribute in diverse ways towards making the law enforcement agents a let-loose, trigger-excited cops of licensed killers.
The Respondent State affirms its written response of 2004 and its oral response of April 2005. It also states that the present submission is a further response to the supplementary address by AJ.

With reference to Odi killings, the Respondent State avers that the citizens of Odi took the case to court claiming compensation for loss of lives which resulted from the killings. It states that the cases are still in court. It also states that the twelve policemen captured and taken hostage by Odi militants while on official assignment were later murdered, despite appeals for their release. It further states that the National Assembly - the legislative arm of Government - set up a Committee which investigated the killings. The Committee, it says, submitted its Report which was under consideration for further action by the Senate of the Federal Republic. It further states that the victims have not complained of any incompetence of the courts in respect of their claims. It says that the victims have faith in the local remedies they have resorted to and that those directly affected by the incident of Odi have not mandated AJ or any other body or person to take action on their behalf.

As regards the Zaki-biam incident, where nineteen soldiers of the Nigeria Army were murdered by militants of Tiv tribal origin, the Respondent State says that the soldiers were sent on a peace-keeping mission to prevent the escalation of an inter-communal crisis between neighbouring tribes in Benue and Taraba States in Nigeria's Middle Belt axis. It states that the soldiers were abducted and brutally murdered by the Tiv militants following an ambush and all entreaties that both the corpses of the slain soldiers and their arms and ammunition be produced were rebuffed. It informs the Commission, that a security operation was, therefore, mounted to recover the bodies of the slain soldiers and to prevent the further deterioration of the situation in the area which was fast approaching the level of anarchy. It avers that it was this operation, which was in pursuance of the duty of the State, to maintain law and order in all parts of the country that AJ erroneously refers to as a 'reprisal mission'.

The Respondent State further informs the Commission that a high-powered 10 - man Judicial Commission of Enquiry headed by the Hon. Justice Okwuchukwu Opene of the Court of Appeal was set up by the Federal Government chaired by a Justice of the Court of Appeal to investigate the incident and any excesses that may have been committed by the militants and the Nigeria military, respectively. It states further that the Commission of Enquiry Report which has been submitted is still passing through the various stages of Government for consideration. Furthermore, it says, some aggrieved citizens from the area have sued the Federal Government of Nigeria at the Federal High Court in Enugu, claiming compensation for loss of lives and properties. It states that in the final judgment, the Court granted compensation in the sum of N 41.8 billion to the victims as compensation. It says that the Federal Government dissatisfied with this judgment appealed against it on the ground that the award was excessive. The matter, it states, is still pending in Court, confirming its earlier position that local remedies were not exhausted by AJ. Furthermore, it states, that the Government commenced negotiations with the victims to reach an amicable settlement. It says that an arbitral panel would soon start sitting on the matter. It says that the victims affected by the incident have not mandated AJ or any other body or person to take action on their behalf.

It informs the Commission that at the Chief of Army Staff Annual Conference, in Makurdi, Benue State, the Chief of Army Staff, Lt. General Luka Yusuf apologized to the people of Benue for the incident.

In a further elaboration on this issue, the Respondent State urges the Commission to note the fact that in resolving violent incidents triggered by ethnic conflicts such as was witnessed in the Zaki-Biam area of Benue State in Nigeria's North-Central Region, there has to be a mix of legal, political and social measures. It says that considering the pattern of evolution of multi-ethnic African countries such as Nigeria, any reasonable political authority will realize that several of the triggers of these ethnic conflagrations are historical in nature, often times to be found in age-long inter-communal feuds that predate the colonial creation called Nigeria. It states that animosities are usually deep-rooted and need to be assuaged through a careful and creative process of social engineering involving dialogue, enlightenment, appeasement, and in extreme cases, prosecution where criminal actions have been committed.

The Respondent State says it notes with a serious sense of responsibility and concern, the allegations of frequent reckless killings by the Nigeria Police Force (NPF). It says that the Government's concern derives primarily from the fact that the NPF was established with the statutory mandate to protect the lives and property of all persons and institutions within the geographical territory of the Federal Republic of Nigeria. It cites Section 4 of the Police Act (Chapter 359, Laws of the Federation of Nigeria 1990) which expressly sets out the primary duty of the Nigeria Police Force as follows:

The police shall be employed for the prevention and detection of crime, the apprehension of offenders, the preservation of law and order, the protection of life and property and the due enforcement of all laws and regulations with which they are directly charged, and shall perform such military duties within or without Nigeria as may be required by them by, or under the authority of, this or any other Act.

It says that in view of these clear and express provisions of the law, the Government will view with serious reservations any allegation that any member of the police force is acting contrary to his mandate and rather than protect lives, has become an instrument for the deprivation of the right to life of any citizen or resident of Nigeria.

It informs the Commission that following detailed investigations, the Government does not deny that such unfortunate incidents have occurred in parts of the country at different times in the last few years. However, it says, it is the official policy and practice that such policemen are usually dismissed from service and prosecuted in the law courts for such crimes. It states that the State does not condone extra-judicial killings by policemen. It argues that several of such cases have been prosecuted in court while other policemen are in custody awaiting trial. It refers the Commission to the recent high-profile 'Apo Six' incident where policemen accused of killing six Nigerians in cold blood were promptly arrested and were put on trial for culpable homicide in Abuja. It also says that the Government has moved further to offer financial compensation of not less than N3.5 million each to the families of the unfortunate victims, following a Judicial Commission of enquiry headed by a Judge of the High Court, Justice Goodluck. It further states that a high powered Federal Government delegation accompanied the corpses of the deceased and handed them over to their relations at a solemn ceremony held in Enugu International Airport.

In the case of the Ajah Four killings, the Respondent State informs the Commission that Shuaibu Bala, Mustapha Mohamed, Sulaiman Idris and Olagunju Lawal had confessed to the crime of armed robbery. It states that the arrested persons were being taken to the scene of the crime by the investigating team when it was ambushed by other members of the gang. It claims that in the ensuing gunfight the Ajah Four were killed. The Respondent State says that in the cases of Messrs Shuaibu Bala, Mustapha Mohammed, Suleiman Idris, Olagunju Lawal and Messrs Celestine Chuke Okoro and Richard Okoroafor allegedly killed by the police between 12 and 13 June 2001 and 29 January 2002, respectively, the Honourable Attorney-General of the Federation requested a briefing from the NPF and the response is being awaited.

In the case of Messrs Celestine Chuke Okoro and Richard Okoroafor allegedly killed by the Police on 29 January 2002, the Respondent State says that the police had received a report of a stolen car. It says that five officers were dispatched to the scene of the alleged theft to investigate the crime when a gunfight ensued between the police and the criminals leading to the deaths of three of the police officers. It agrees that a stray bullet hit and killed one person whose name and address was unknown. It states that it was clear that the situation portrayed a complete breakdown of law and order. These cases, it avers, are being investigated and it is expected that the culprits will be brought to justice at the end.

It concludes that in the light of the above official policy, it is wrong to insinuate, as AJ has attempted, that the Nigeria State condones such extra-judicial killings wherever they occur. In addition, it is says, Nigerian law provides extensively for both civil and criminal remedies where there have been allegations of extra-judicial killings against any person or institution. It says that there is no evidence in the matters raised by AJ that the aggrieved persons have had a recourse to the law courts to seek such judicial reliefs, lending credence to Nigeria's submission that local remedies were not exhausted by the Complainant or any legal agent on their behalf before this matter was prematurely referred to the Commission contrary to Article 56 of the Charter of the African Commission.

The Respondent State says that contrary to the statement made at Page 2 of AJ's Supplementary Address in respect of vigilante groups, the Government has reiterated the fact that all such vigilante groups that bear arms, remain proscribed under the extant laws. Indeed, it avers, that the Government has commenced the prosecution of some leaders of such groups for various crimes against the State, including Mujaheddin Dokubo Asari of the Niger Delta Volunteer Force (Treason, before the Federal High Court, Abuja), Ralph Uwazurike of the Movement for the Actualization of the Sovereign State of Biafra (Treason, before the Federal High Court, Abuja) and Dr Frederick Fashehun / Chief Gani Adams of the Odua Peoples' Congress (Murder/ Unlawful Possession of Firearms, before the Lagos State High Court), respectively. It concludes that it is, therefore, incorrect to say that the vigilante groups are operating with State indulgence.

The Respondent State argues that AJ depended largely on media reports to gather the evidence adduced, as admitted by it at Page 10 of its Supplementary Address. It argues that Nigeria is not aware that AJ was called upon to intervene by any of the injured parties, nor did it go to the alleged scenes of the incidents mentioned, but depended largely on the aforesaid media reports and speculations to make its submissions contrary to the provisions of Article 56(4) of the Charter.

With regard to AJ's submission on the issue of 'waiver' of Article 56(5) of the Charter which is based on the allegation of massive extra-judicial killings, the Respondent State argues that the alleged incident occurred only once in 1999 at Odi and had been addressed in this submission. It avers that the Zaki-Biam incident of 2002 was equally a single occurrence and again, has been addressed in this submission. The Respondent State further says that the alleged cases cited by AJ occurred at different periods and in different places and cannot be described as 'massive and widespread'.

Based on the fore-going submission, it says, the application for waiver under Article 58(1) should not have been entertained on the ground that it is not a waiver to Article 56(5). It argues that the waiver to Article 56(5) can only be entertained if it is shown that recourse to local remedy was unduly prolonged. It also argues that there is no evidence that the Complainant took recourse to any local remedy let alone such remedy being unduly prolonged. Article 56, it avers, is mandatory, succinct and clear. Furthermore, it claims, Article 58 does not dispense with the requirements of Article 56 and therefore, Nigeria reaffirms her submission to the effect that Access to Justice has not exhausted local remedies.

Reacting to the submission by AJ at Page 11 of its submission, the Respondent State says it is a flagrant exaggeration of the situation in Nigeria. It states that allusion by AJ to massive human rights violations in Nigeria as occasioned by the Odi, Zaki-Biam and Choba incidents contained in its submission is an exaggeration. It says that it can only be construed as an attempt to embarrass the Government of Nigeria, underscored not only by the reluctance and impatience of AJ to exploit and exhaust local remedies to issues raised, as well as genuinely intervening on behalf of the injured parties, but also by the fact that AJ intends to exploit Article 58(1) of the African Charter to take the case to the Assembly of Heads of State and Government without thorough and in-depth investigation.

The Respondent State argues that all these point to the fact that the ultimate intent of the write-up by AJ is not to seek remedies for any violation of human rights, wherever they may have occurred in Nigeria, but to create a forum for the disparagement of the Government and its President who was the Chairperson of the African Union. Citing 56(3) it notes with much regret that the President of the Federal Republic of Nigeria has been insolently and disparagingly referred to in AJ's submission as well as in its oral presentation. It says that the person and office of the President of the Federal Republic of Nigeria should be distinguished from the Nigerian State as an entity even in cases of genuine complaints against the country.
It implores the Commission to refrain from assisting AJ achieve its aim which is not in consonance with the objectives for which the Commission was set up.

In the case of Inspector Abah Olobi allegedly killed by Police Constable Yohanna Akaji and Sergeant Yakubu Biri on 12 October 1997, in Bassa Local Government Area of Plateau State, the Respondent State informs the Commission that the accused persons were arrested and arraigned before the High Court of Plateau State on a charge of Murder. It says that the accused persons pleaded not guilty to the five charges against them. After the plea of the accused was taken on 23 July 1996, the Commission was informed, a lengthy strike action embarked upon by Civil Servants in Plateau State contributed to the delay in the commencement of hearing in the case, coupled with the fact that the prosecution encountered difficulties in serving summonses on the witnesses for the prosecution. It further states that regrettably, the Counsel (Prosecutor) handling the case died and the Plateau State Ministry of Justice was unable, unfortunately to re-assign the case. another Counsel (due to a paucity of Counsel) between the period of 21 June and 29 November 2001 when the case was struck out for want of diligent prosecution.

The Respondent State argues that, whatever the case, its municipal system was not exhausted by the Complainant. It states that the Plateau State Ministry of Justice made a request to the State Judiciary for the re-assignment of the case as the Judge handling the case is no longer in service, while the police have been directed to re-arrest the accused persons. It also says that detectives are on their trail and they should soon be taken into custody. These steps, it says are pre-conditions for either revisiting the struck-out case or filing fresh charges against the accused persons.

The Respondent State admits that the case of Miss Olajumoke is a rather pathetic and unfortunate incident, which the Government itself has viewed with sympathy and deep concern. It relates the facts as follows as ascertained by Nigeria Police Force conducting the investigations:

In the above matter, the Respondent State says that Miss Olajumoke, was allegedly killed by officers of the NPF in Lagos State on 14 June 2000, whilst one Ms Juliana Obiajulu was allegedly killed by one Sergeant Matthew Marontonu of the Nigeria Police Force on 30 May 2000. It says that both cases are still pending before the Federal High Court, Lagos and the Attorney-General of the Federation and the Minister of Justice being a party to these suits requested for briefing from the NPF to enable him take appropriate action and ensure that justice is done. In response, the NPF have indicated their intention to reach an out-of-court settlement with the families of the deceased persons.

The Complainant states that this Communication is based primarily on incidences of rampant extra-judicial killings prevalent in Nigeria and enumerated in its earlier submission. It says that the practice of extra-judicial killing in Nigeria is systematic, entrenched and routine. In other words, it avers, grave human rights violations have persisted relentlessly and several Nigerians lose their lives to extra-legal, arbitrary and summary executions by law enforcement agents while the Nigerian Government remains aloof and indifferent to these abuses. It states that despite being a signatory to many international treaties, including the African Charter, the Government has contrary to its provisions failed to respect, protect and safeguard the right to life.

It states that between 1999 and 2004, state agents who acting on Presidential orders perpetrated serious violations of the right to life. It states that overwhelming pogroms in Odi, Choba, Zaki Biam and in the Niger Delta region in South-South Nigeria depict with shocking details state authorship of the largest incidents of extra-judicial killings in Nigeria, which by reputable local and international accounts run into several thousands.

It states that while the Ajah 4 killings illustrates how the police deploys its institutional strength to hush (through threats of assassinations) demands for investigations by families of victims, the Ayuba Parakoyi case on the other hand illustrates how the police manipulate investigations to help police officers escape with lesser indictments for serious crimes. It says that Parakoyi was killed in the full glare of several witnesses in a capacity-filled stadium when the deceased disputed with a police officer over who should keep a promotion T-shirt. The police officer resolved the dispute with a gunshot from his service pistol and later claimed that the gun accidentally exploded when the deceased attempted to wrest it from him. Police investigations into the killing relied on one witness who corroborated this account, and subsequently presented a report that left the Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP) with only one option, to recommend prosecution for manslaughter rather than murder. The DPP however had this to say about police investigation into the killing: "We must however observe that the police did not conduct a proper investigation into this case before sending the case file as they are duty bound to obtain statements of other eye-witnesses in order to give a clearer picture of the event..."

The Complainant claims that cases like the above are abound, but the police have not only demonstrated unwillingness to investigate and prosecute erring officers, they have shown disregard for civilian mechanisms of oversights, and for judicial processes and inquiries. It accuses the police of habitually shunning judicial processes and making independent attempts at engaging these processes frustrating.

It says that generally, the exercise of the unfettered control that the police enjoy over investigative processes does not conform to international standards such as those set by the United Nations Principles on the Effective Prevention Investigation of Extra-Legal, Arbitrary and Summary Execution. It claims that police investigative procedures not only detract from these standards, they make no pretence at sustaining the detraction. It alleges that most cases of killings by the police escape investigations, and outcomes of the few investigations conducted are hardly ever made public in line with the above standards, or disclosed to the families of the victims.

The Complainant further claims that in paragraph 7 of the Government written response on the Merit, it expressly admitted the occurrence of extra-judicial killings within the country and alleged that several police men have been dismissed and prosecuted in connection to extrajudicial killings. However, it says, the Government did not provide evidence of what it has done to redress police killings as alleged by the Complainant. It also says that the Government has failed to provide proof of the prosecutions they allege or adduce evidence of law enforcement officers who were successfully prosecuted. Therefore, it says, the claims by the Government are vague and unsubstantiated assertions calculated to mislead the African Commission into believing that it is redressing the right to life violations in Nigeria as it should. It maintains, that prosecutions for extra-judicial killings by policemen are isolated and far from what it ought to be, given the records of abusive killings.

The Complainant affirms that the Government, by its systematic failure to carry out thorough, impartial investigation into cases of killings by law enforcement officers, has violated the provisions of the African Charter. Citing Communication 74/92 Commission Nationale des Droits de l'Homme et des Libertés/Chad, it argues that the Commission stated that when a government fails to investigate assassinations or prosecute those concerned it violates of Article 7 of the Charter.

It states that the Government alleged in paragraphs 4 and 5 of its written response on the Merit that a panel of inquiry was set up to look into the Odi killing and that the Government is looking into the report, while an arbitration panel for the consideration of compensation to be paid to victims of Zaki-Biam killing will soon be set up. Furthermore, it states, the Government alleged that Odi and Zaki-Biam indigenes have instituted lawsuits for damages. It argues that it is depressing and anti-human rights for a Government to say that it is still considering the panel's report or still planning on setting up a panel for the consideration of compensation after seven to ten years of the massive killings in Odi and Zaki-Biam. It submits that seven years to ten years is too long for the report to still be under consideration or the panel for compensation to be still in- formation. It insists that the delay is not only inexcusable, it smacks of a culture that places little regard on human life. It avers that responses to events concerning extra-judicial killings, particularly with respect to investigation and punishment of perpetrators must be prompt.
The Respondent State did not respond to this additional response from the Complainant.

The Complainant has based its claims against the Respondent State on the violations of Articles 1, 2, 4, 6 7, 9 13 and 16 of the African Charter. The Complainant has not canvassed its cause under the articles which it says have been violated by the Respondent State. The Respondent State has similarly not addressed or articulated its responses under the relevant articles for which it is being accused of violating. That will, however, not prevent the Commission from analyzing the matter and (not) finding a violation of the African Charter if there was (not) one. The narrative from both parties is clear enough to allow the African Commission to proceed with a determination on the Merits.

The African Commission also notes that in its submission on the Merits (see for example paras: 103, 105, 114, 116, 118, 119, 120), the Respondent State still refers to provisions in Article 56 and the fact that AJ has taken an actio popularis position in this Communication. Those arguments are not addressed as it pertains to arguments which have been addressed and settled at the Admissibility stage.

Article 4 of the African Charter guarantees that every human being is entitled to respect for his life and the integrity of his person and that any harm inflicted against any person constitutes a violation of the physical integrity of that person.

The Respondent State did not respond to all the accusations levied against it. It says that the alleged cases cited by AJ occurred at different periods and in different places and cannot be described as 'massive and widespread'. It further states (without providing any proof) that it has already submitted that the identified cases of violations by law - enforcement agents have been addressed. In some of the incidences, the Respondent State has admitted excesses from some of its officers, but states (without providing any evidence of real concrete action that is being taken), that the matters are being investigated or are before the courts. For example, in the case of the Ajah Four allegedly killed by the NPF between 12 and 13 June 2001 and January 29 2002, the Respondent State says that the Attorney-General of the Federation requested a briefing from the NPF and the response is being awaited; in the case of Ms Olajumoke, allegedly killed by the NPF in Lagos State on 14 June 2000, and Ms Juliana Obiajulu allegedly killed on 30 May 2000, the Respondent State says that both cases (by the time the Complaint was lodged at the African Commission) are still pending before the Federal High Court. In the case of Messrs Celestine Chuke Okoro and Richard Okoroafor allegedly killed by the Police on 29 January 2002, the Respondent State says that the case is being investigated and it is expected that the culprits will be brought to justice at the end.

In the case of Inspector Abah Olobi allegedly killed on 12 October 1997, the Respondent State says that a lengthy strike action embarked upon by Civil Servants in Plateau State contributed to the delay in the commencement of hearing in the case. It has not informed the Commission of the eventual outcome.

However, before determining whether there has been a violation of Article 4, it is important to understand what mischief the article intends to cure. In Communication 25/89-47/90-56/91-100/93 : Free Legal Assistance Group, Lawyers' Committee for Human Rights, Union Interafricaine des Droits de l'Homme, Les Témoins de Jehovah / DRC, the Commission stated that the article is intended to protect the right to life. This prompts the question: what then is a violation of the right to life? In Communication 54/91-61/91-96/93-98/93-164/97_196/97-210/98 : Malawi African Association, Amnesty International, Ms Sarr Diop, Union interafricaine des droits de l'Homme and RADDHO, Collectif des veuves et ayants-Droit, Association mauritanienne des droits de l'Homme / Mauritania, the Commission stated that arbitrary executions and subjecting people to torture to the point of death point to a shocking lack of respect for life, and constitutes a violation of Article 4.

The Commission further stated in Gabriel Shumba v Zimbabwe that the term 'the right to life' – is a phrase that describes the belief that a human being has an essential right to live, particularly that a human being has the right not to be killed by another human being. It said that Article 4 "is the fulcrum of all other rights, the fountain through which other rights flow, and any violation of this right without due process amounts to arbitrary deprivation of life" - that states not only have to refrain from intentional and unlawful deprivation of life, but must also take appropriate steps to safeguard the lives of those within its jurisdiction. It further said that the right enshrined in this article is the supreme right of the human being. It follows that the deprivation of life by the authorities of the state is a matter of the utmost gravity. The requirements that the right shall be protected by law and that no one shall be arbitrarily deprived of his life mean that the law must strictly control and limit the circumstances in which a person may be deprived of his life arbitrarily.

The Commission notes that while the Complainant alleges various and serious incidences of extra-judicial killings, it has also been able to provide evidences of Government and or police inaction to support many of its allegations. It has for example, filed civil action damages after efforts to prompt police investigations in the Olajumoke case, provided witness testimonies, written letters to the (police) authorities in Ajah Four killings, instituted inquests into the Richard Okoro and Celestine Okoroafor case, though the police refused to participate. In the case of Richard Okoro and Celestine Okoroafor according to the papers submitted by the Complainant to the Commission, the Coroner found that the policemen perpetrated the killings. The police refused to participate in that inquest.

The Commission also notes that the Respondent State does not dispute many of the citations and in its Merit brief admitted that some of its officers may have been implicated in extra-judicial killings. In paragraph 7 of its Merit brief it stated that "on the allegation of frequent reckless killings by the police, the Nigerian Government does not deny that such unfortunate incidents have occurred in parts of the country at different times." It however states that the Government does not have a policy of condoning such extra-judicial killings by policemen. It further admitted in paragraph 12, of its submission, while attempting to rebut the allegation of widespread impunity in the police force, categorized extra-judicial killings as events that occurred at different periods and places. The Respondent State further avers that several policemen have been dismissed and prosecuted in connection to extrajudicial killings.

The Commission is of the view that much of the defence of the Respondent State lacks any commitment to the inviolability of human lives and the protection of human rights. Article 4 is clear. It is intended not only to prohibit absolutely the arbitrary taking of life by the State, but by implication, any life which allegedly has been taken arbitrarily, should be investigated and the violator(s) brought to justice. It notes that the Respondent State did not provide evidence of what it has done to redress the various police killings as alleged by the Complainant. It also notes that the Respondent State has failed to provide evidence of the prosecutions they allege or adduce evidence of law enforcement officers who were successfully prosecuted. The Commission is of the view that prosecutions for extra-judicial killings by policemen are isolated and far from what it ought to be, given the numerous records of abusive killings, which has been enumerated by the Complainant. The Commission is of the view that the claims by the Government are not clear and are unsubstantiated with the intention to create the impression that it is redressing the right to life violations as it should. The Commission is left with alternative but to agree with the Complainant that there seems to be a deeply entrenched culture of brutality and impunity within the police force coupled with a culture of silence and cover-ups which is in total breach of their duty as a police force.

The Commission agrees with the Complainant that the Respondent State has a duty to investigate violations of human rights and punish those responsible for the violations where those responsible are its agents or third parties. The Commission finds it disturbing that the numerous allegations of violations of Article 4 (which it has not denied) that is levied against it cannot be accidental, but stem from a deep and worrying culture of police violence and a cavalier attitude for the lives of other citizens. It notes that investigations on extra-judicial killings are exclusively investigable by the police under existing laws in Nigeria and the few investigations conducted by the police were done after protracted public insistence and the findings were either not publicized, or were often inconclusive. The Commission also notes the various observations of the Special Rapporteur on Summary or Extra-Judicial Executions quoted by the Complainant and has to agree that there is a pervading culture of impunity within the police force. It also notes that effective remedies do not exist to review police decisions, or where investigations have been carried out, there are no effective ways to bring out the truth.

The Commission for example notes that the Ajah Four killings, the Ayuba Parakoyi cases, illustrates how the police deploys its institutional strength to suppress (through threats of assassinations) demands for investigations by families of victims and how the police can manipulate investigations to help police officers escape with lesser indictments for serious crimes. The Commission agrees with the Complainant that cases like the above abound, where the police have not only demonstrated unwillingness to investigate and prosecute erring officers, but have also shown disregard for civilian mechanisms of oversights, and for judicial processes and inquiries. The Commission, for example notes the cases of Wale Agagu (not addressed by the Respondent State) and Mr. Ifezina who was tortured to death (not addressed by the Respondent State) and has to reach only one conclusion – that the incidences are a total violation of Article 4 of the African Charter. In this regard, it is instructive to note that in Communication 205/97: Kazeem Aminu v Nigeria, the Commission laid down a general principle that it is the duty of the State Party to apprehend persons whom it reasonably believes have committed or are in the process of committing offences recognized by its laws. However, such arrests and/or detentions must be in accordance with known laws, which in turn must be in accordance with the provisions of the Charter. The State is not given a license to unlawfully kill its citizens and then use threats and sham investigations to cover its crimes.

The Commission also agrees that the Respondent State has failed to provide effective remedies for the relatives of families of the victim. It emphasizes that the duty to make reparation to victims or families of victims of human rights violations exists under international law and has been recognized by the African Commission. The Complainant cites Communication 59/91, Louis Emgba Mekongo/ Cameroon where the Commission held that the "complainant is entitled to reparations for the prejudice he has suffered". The Commission agrees with the Complainant that despite being aware of the unlawful killings of hundreds of people (possibly even thousands) mentioned by the Complainant, the Respondent State has failed to make reparation to the families of victims of these violations even where it has expressly accepted that the killings were unlawful, or has impliedly done so by commencing prosecution against those implicated in the killing. The Commission notes with regrets that even in the one case where the Respondent State conceded that it was vicariously responsible for the action of its officers in the Zaki-Baim case and where the Federal High Court in Enugu ordered a ₦41.8 billion ($) compensation, it has decided to appeal the amount given to the relatives of the deceased.

On the Odi killings, the Commission further notes the response from the Respondent State in paragraphs 4 and 5 of its written response on the Merits that a panel of inquiry was set up to look into the Odi killing and that the Government is looking into the report, while an arbitral panel for the consideration of compensation to be paid to victims of Zaki-Biam killing will soon be set up. Furthermore, it notes the reply of the Respondent State that Odi and Zaki-Biam indigenes have instituted lawsuits for damages. The Commission agrees with the Complainant that it is anti-human rights for a Government to say that it is still considering the panel's report or still planning on setting up a panel for the consideration of compensation after seven to ten years of the killings in Odi and Zaki-Biam. It further agrees that seven years to ten years is far too long for the report to still be under consideration or the panel for compensation to still be established. The Commission wishes to state that such the delays are inexcusable, bordering on a culture that places little regard for human life, for which Article 4 was put in place. It agrees with the Complainant that responses to events concerning extra-judicial killings, particularly with respect to investigation and punishment of perpetrators must be prompt.

The Commission wishes to state that this Communication contains the names of various people who were victims of extra-judicial killings or attempted attacks against their physical integrity, and acts of intimidation. The Respondent State did not deny many of the allegations. Also, the Respondent State has never published the results of any the Commission of Enquiry set up following the numerous allegations levied against it nor did it concretely identify the perpetrators of the various offences or take any measures against them. In conformity with its own jurisprudence which states that "whenever allegations of human rights abuses are not contested by the accused State, ... the Commission shall decide on the basis of the facts provided by the plaintiff and treat such facts as they are presented to it." The Commission therefore applies the same reasoning to the facts related in the present communication. The Commission would also like to reiterate a fundamental principle proclaimed in Article 1 of the Charter that not only do the States Parties recognize the rights, duties and freedoms enshrined in the Charter they also commit themselves to respect them and to take measures to give effect to them. In other words, if a State Party fails to ensure respect of the rights contained in the African Charter, this constitutes a violation of Article 4 of the Charter, even if the State or its agents were not the perpetrators of the violation.

The Complainant did not specifically canvass a violation of Article 5 of the African Charter, though it gave detailed and graphic accounts of instances of torture. Upon reading the submission which was not contested by the Respondent State, the Commission is of the view that it has to address itself to this article. But is the Commission able to address a violation under a specific article that has not been specifically canvassed by the Complainant? The Commission answers that question in the affirmative. The objective of the African Charter and indeed the Commission is to promote and protect human rights in the continent. Would it not defeat the purpose and entire spirit of the Charter, if a glaring and gross human rights violation is not addressed just because a Complaint, for whatever reason, fails to canvass the violation under a specific article? In the instant case, the Complainant has informed the Commission of instances of torture which it wants the Commission to address. Yes, it did not cite such cases under Article 5 of the Charter, but it wants the Commission to address them. The Commission does so under the relevant Article 5.

The Commission wishes to further state that object and purpose of human rights bodies and treaties and the requirement of effectiveness mean that a body like the Commission and a treaty like the Charter must not be narrowly construed. For example in Aminu v. Nigeria, the Complainant was "hiding for fear of his life". The Commission held that "[i]t would be a narrow interpretation of this right to think that it can only be violated when one is deprived of it." In that regard it is always necessary to choose the alternative that is most favorable to protection of the rights based on the principle of the rule most favorable to the human being" - usually referred to as the pro homine principle. The Charter should be seen as a living instrument protecting the individual against the threats of the future, as well as against the threats of the past.

The Commission will, thus examine the alleged violations under Article 5. Article 5 guarantees respect for the dignity inherent in the human person and the recognition of his legal status. This Article further prohibits all forms of exploitation and degradation of man, particularly slavery, slave trade, torture cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment and treatment. The guarantee of the physical integrity and security of the person is also enshrined in Article 6 of the African Charter.

Before examining Article 5 in relation to the instant matter, it must be stated that the Commission takes an uncompromising stand against torture, inhuman and degrading treatment. In this regard, it has developed Guidelines (Robben Island Guidelines for the Prohibition and Prevention of torture in Africa) to assist states to address cases of torture including its criminalization. The Guide is a set of norms that regulate the way states can exercise powers of detention, setting out the minimum standards for conditions of detention, and provide guidelines as to how those deprived of their liberty should be treated. The Guidelines also require states to bring to justice those responsible for acts of torture or ill-treatment.

In Gabriel Shumba v Zimbabwe the Commission noted that it is not a mistake that along with genocide, torture is the only crime that every state must punish, no matter who commits it or where. It further stated in Communication 279/03-296/05: Sudan Human Rights Organization & Centre on Housing Rights and Evictions (COHRE) v Sudan, that while the African Charter does not define the meaning of the words, or the phrase "torture or degrading treatment or punishment, Article 5 is aimed at the protection of both the dignity of the human person, and the physical and mental integrity of the individual..." The African Commission further went to state in Communication 279/03-296/05 that torture constitutes the intentional and systematic infliction of physical or psychological pain and suffering in order to punish, intimidate or gather information.

In the instant Communication, the Complainant has enumerated the cases of Mr Ifezina and Wale Agagu, both not responded to by the Respondent State. In the case of Mr Ifezina, the Complainant gave graphic details of the ordeals he was put through whilst he was in police custody in 2004. He was stripped naked, his legs folded upwards to his knees and tied at the ankles, his arms were raised upwards and tied together at the wrists. A pipe attached at the ends to a rope hanging from ceiling fan hook in the ceiling, was passed between both legs and both arms. He was then raised towards the ceiling by pulling at the loose ends of the rope, until he was suspended in the air in the form of a human bow – a position that caused excruciating pain all over the body but particularly in the shoulders, the spine and the waist. Whilst Mr Ifezina was suffering this pain, the interrogating officer then began to insert and withdraw an unsterilized needle into and out of his penis through the urinary tract, while asking him questions. Blood coursed out of Ifezina's genitals in the meanwhile and spattered the floor while he helplessly screamed from pain. The penis which became swollen subsequently oozed and emitted rancid pus. The police neither treated him nor allowed him treatment. He eventually died.

Article 5 of the African Charter is clear. It prohibits absolutely any form of the ill-treatment or infliction of physical or psychological pain and suffering. The torture of Mr Ifezina and and ill-treatment of Wale Agagu is clearly a violation of Article 5. The Commission has in the past indicated that in terms of Article 5 of the African Charter, every person deprived of his or her liberty has the right to be detained in conditions compatible with his or her personal dignity, and the state must guarantee that person the right to life and to humane treatment. Consequently, since the state is the institution responsible for detention establishments, it is the guarantor of these rights of the prisoners. In the instant cases, the two victims died in police custody through gross mistreatment and intentional infliction of pain and suffering, which has not been denied by the Respondent State. It agrees with the Complainant that the Respondent State has failed in its duty to protect its citizens in the aforementioned cases.

The African Commission agrees that the Complainant has submitted more than adequate evidences to support the allegations of torture and ill-treatment by the Nigerian police, which at least should have prompted an official investigation. In the instant case the Respondent State did not even address the very serious allegations of the torture of Mr Ifezina and the ill-treatment of Wale Agagu. The African Commission also agrees with the Complainant that in seeking to refute the allegations, it is not sufficient for the Respondent State to simply argue that they are unsubstantiated when they are supported by range of documentation. Rather, the Respondent State must provide evidence to the contrary.

As has been stated supra the burden of proof rests on the Government and where the Government provides no evidence to contradict an allegation of human rights violation made against it, the African Commission will take it as proven, or at the least probable or plausible.
Declares that the Respondent State has violated the right not to be subjected to torture as recognized in Article 5 of the African Charter.

Article 6 of the African Charter states that every individual shall have the right to liberty and to the security of his person and that no one may be deprived of his freedom except for reasons and conditions previously laid down by law. In particular, no one may be arbitrarily arrested or detained. The Complainant has given numerous instances where members of the police force have arbitrarily detained victims, eventually leading to their deaths. The case of Wale, the Apo Six, the Ajah Four and many more enumerated in the Complainant various submissions.

The African Commission has also stated that simply because an arrest is carried out does not necessarily amount to a violation of Article 6. In Communication 48/90-50/91-52/91-89/93: Amnesty International, Comité Loosli Bachelard, Lawyers' Committee for Human Rights, Association of Members of the Episcopal Conference of East Africa v Sudan, the African Commission stated that this article must be interpreted in such a way as to permit arrests only in the exercise of powers normally granted to the security forces in a democratic society.

According to the African Commission's settled case-law, the presumption under Article 6 is in favour of release. As established in the Jawara case the second limb of Article 6 does not give judicial authorities a choice between either bringing an accused to trial within a reasonable time or granting him provisional release pending trial. Until conviction, s/he must be presumed innocent, and the purpose of the provision under consideration is essentially to require his provisional release once his continuing detention ceases to be reasonable.

In the instant Communication, the Commission notes that all of the arrestees eventually died in prison. They were never given the opportunity to defend themselves before a competent court and the Respondent State did not respond to the allegations of torture and false imprisonment. The Commission has, however, laid down a general principle in Communication 101/93 with respect to freedom of association that competent authorities should not enact provisions or take any actions which limit the exercise of this freedom. This principle applies not only to freedom of association but also to all other rights and freedoms, including the right not to be arbitrarily arrested and detained. The Commission finds that the arrests and detention of the aforementioned persons is inconsistent with Nigeria's obligations under the African Charter. They constitute arbitrary deprivation of liberty and a violation of Article 6 of the Charter.
